558fcb3948ca1986: From the Tengku Ampuan of Pahang, Tunku Azizah Aminah Maimunah Iskandariah Before I begin, I would like to congratulate Muzium Negeri Pahang on its 50th anniversary, its Golden Jubilee.

On this occasion, I remember with gratitude my late father-in-law, Almarhum Sultan Haji Ahmad Shah, who made Istana Kota Beram available to become a museum. That decision gave our heritage a home, and the museum has come a very long way since then.
So has its director.

I still remember Dato' Farid, the Dato Setia Jasa, as a skinny young man, fresh out of university. To me, he was practically a little boy. Today, he has grown in experience, confidence and wisdom, and acquired a few white hairs along the way.
I hope the museum deserves most of the credit for his wisdom, and that I am not entirely responsible for the white hairs!
But seriously, Farid has grown with this museum. I congratulate him on the ideas, dedication and vision he has brought to it, and on the ideas and vision he continues to have.
Our museum is increasingly talked about, and that makes me proud.

A museum must keep moving. It should inform and welcome people. Its exhibitions should change, giving visitors something new to discover and a reason to return. It should attract families, students, scholars and people who may never have thought that a museum was a place for them.
It should make people feel that their history belongs to them.
That is what I believe Muzium Pahang has worked hard to achieve.
My thanks also go to the staff whose work makes all this possible, and to the Pahang State Government for understanding our ambitions and continuing to support us.
Although, with a self-confessed control freak as the museum’s royal patron, perhaps they have not always had much choice!

This is also where a royal consort has work to do. Alongside the Sultan’s responsibilities, there is a contribution we can make through supporting our heritage, encouraging its practitioners and helping ensure that what we have inherited reaches another generation.
For me, that work comes from love. Patronage means taking an interest, listening, learning and being willing to sit with the people doing the work. Sometimes, quite literally, on the floor.
To everyone who has helped this museum reach its Golden Jubilee, thank you.
I must also confess that I feel rather humbled standing before so many distinguished scholars, each a master in his or her field.
And yes, a little nervous.

This is a subject about which many of you have spent your professional lives thinking and writing. I come before you with my own experience, my research and a great love for what I have been studying.
I have also realised that this seminar is being conducted in Malay, and I have prepared my keynote in English.
I do have a Malay translation. But I find that the English version allows me to express some of these thoughts more naturally.
Dato' Farid once told me, “Tuanku, speak in your mother tongue.”
I told him, “Yes, that is exactly what I am doing. My mother is English!”

There are thoughts that come to me more readily in English, and others that find their expression in Malay. So please allow me to speak in the language in which I can best share these reflections with you. And if some Malay finds its way in, that too is part of how I think.
This seminar has a very special place in my heart because it concerns a subject that has become so important to me: the Hukum Kanun of the Malay world, our Laws.
Through the Hukum Kanun Pahang, I discovered history. But I also discovered something within myself.

It challenged me, gave direction to my curiosity and helped me recognise what I was capable of achieving through study. For me, the work I have done on the Hukum Kanun Pahang is my greatest personal achievement.
It has changed the way I see things.

These days, whatever I am watching, reading or discussing, I seem to find myself comparing it with the Hukum Kanun Pahang. My family must sometimes wonder whether I can still have a conversation without bringing it into the discussion.
But that is what happens when a subject takes hold of your mind and your heart. You begin to recognise connections you had not seen before.
I thank Allah for leading me to that discovery, and for the opportunity to learn from it.
The keynote I am about to share grew from one such connection.
Before Tun Abdul Razak Hussein became Prime Minister, he was already a Shahbandar.

Tunku Azizah Aminah Maimunah Iskandariah holds a master’s degree from the International Institute of Islamic Thought and Civilisation (ISTAC), International Islamic University Malaysia, and is currently a PhD candidate at ISTAC-IIUM.
feb73f849ef2d58e: From Ravinder Singh
While education minister Fadhlina Sidek accurately stated that school caning was still legally allowed, current disciplinary frameworks are clearly falling short.
The regulations meant to ensure a safe and conducive learning environment have not prevented a severe decline in student behaviour, culminating in tragic instances of fatal school violence.
This crisis raises a critical question: have our existing school discipline rules completely failed?
The road to hell begins with good intentions

The Education (School Discipline) Regulations 1959 of Malaysia governs student discipline and corporal punishment in public schools. The red tape that schools must comply with in using the cane makes caning totally useless.

Only the head teacher or a designated teacher can use the cane, not the class teacher; caning must be done privately; another teacher must be present as a witness; details such as the child’s name, offence, punishment, date and time must be recorded.
As the then assistant headmaster of SK Tunku Abdul Halim in Alor Setar, I witnessed a dramatic shift in our school’s trajectory.

It was the premier primary school in northern Kedah during the 1950s and 1960s, but by 1990, when I took charge, it had become one of the worst. Faced with this crisis, I had two choices: allow the decay to continue or use the cane on my own terms to restore order.
I chose to do it my way, even though it bypassed standard disciplinary regulations. The approach worked, and I want to share that experience here.
Mayhem reigned in this school. Unbearable noise, unsightly litter everywhere, teachers screaming at children, children leaving classrooms and loitering, pushing and shoving at the canteen.

I was in total disbelief when the school head said at a staff meeting that “here we practice democracy”. This was clearly directed at me for controlling the “democracy” that children had been given the freedom to practice and pull the school down into the gutter.
Judicious use of the cane worked a miracle

Having given teachers a set of my own “classroom and child management rules” to be strictly implemented, I started my daily two rounds of corridor walking with a cane in hand for on-the-spot shock-giving to the brain to trigger re-wiring of the bad behaviour connections to good.
Of the 600 plus children in this boys’ school, hardly 10% needed the cure. The rest got the clear message that rules had to be obeyed; their previous “democratic” ways were not acceptable to me.
A light cane is most effective during early childhood, that is in pre-school and primary school, which is the critical habit-forming age. Not every child requires it.
However, for those who do, the physical sting serves as a necessary shock, breaking negative behavioural patterns and prompting them to re-evaluate their actions.
It works the same way that cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) does to shock the heart to start functioning again. Like CPR, the cane must be administered immediately after the event, without delay.
The cane was used only on the palms. One parent confronted me as his Year 3 son had a cane mark on his wrist because the boy had pulled his hand away.
“Do you have the authority to cane children?”
“Yes,” I said, as I told him I would not allow his son to disrupt a class of over 30, running around and pulling other children’s books and pencils while they did their work.
He could take his son to another school if he so wished. The son was soon back in school, a changed person. I set the standard, the parents followed.

On the first school day of the new year, I had a dialogue with the parents in the hall. I reminded them of this school’s excellent status in the 1950s and 1960s, and its shameful status now, all because discipline had not been strictly maintained.
To achieve good academic performance, the prerequisite was good discipline. If teachers had to use the cane to restore discipline, it was for the good of the children.
They gave me unanimous support, and I never had an issue with any of them as long as I was there. Teachers were happy they could conduct lessons with children paying attention.

When I left one and a half years later it took just one week for “democracy” to return to the school. It was heartbreaking that no one could continue maintaining the discipline that I had taken so much trouble to restore within three months of taking charge.
False theories surrounding child disciplining issues
There is not a single study of an actual hands-on use of the cane in real-life situations like I did. All other “studies” are based on the results of wrongful use of the cane.
This is like compiling a list of botched medical surgeries and concluding that surgeries can cause deaths and paralysis and therefore should be banned.
In my own way I proved that a light cane, properly used, is an excellent tool for maintaining discipline in primary school. Then, strict discipline has to be maintained in secondary schools.
The education ministry should not dismiss the “grandfathers’ way” of disciplining children. If schools set the discipline standard, parents will respect it and do their part.
When schools accept indiscipline, parents think that is normal and cannot accept when any teacher disciplines their child.
Get it right — every school must set and enforce strict discipline. Only when schools stop accepting indiscipline will parents take the discipline of their children seriously.
Ravinder Singh is an FMT reader.

b482ac6e1114a80c: Saya petik laporan Berita Harian siaran 22 Okt lalu mengenai ucapan Nik Muhammad Zawawi Salleh, Ahli Parlimen PAS bagi Pasir Putih, yakni ketika beliau membahas Rang Undang-undang Perbekalan 2027 di Parlimen. Beliau gesa kerajaan kurangkan pemberian bantuan tunai dan beri lebih tumpuan kepada usaha memperkasakan rakyat supaya mampu menjana pendapatan sendiri untuk jangka panjang. Ada yang saya setuju, dan ada tidak.

Kata Zawawi, kerajaan perlu mendidik rakyat supaya berusaha mencipta peluang dan bekerja untuk meningkatkan kehidupan. Bagi saya, rakyat tidak perlu diajar oleh kerajaan. Tidak perlu kerajaan berkhutbah menggesa rakyat 'cipta peluang' dan 'kerja' untuk tingkatkan tahap kehidupan, sebab sememangnya rakyat terutama golongan miskin tahu itu semua. Mereka tahu apa yang perlu dilakukan untuk survive dan tingkatkan kehidupan.
That's what they have been doing all this while.

Sememangnya rakyat sentiasa bekerja (dengan keras) serta mencari dan mengintai peluang untuk senang dan menikmati lebih kesenangan. They don’t need the government to lecture or teach what they have to do to improve their livelihood.

Berkata lagi Zawawi: "kalau kita ada peruntukan, rakyat kita bagi 'kail', jangan kita bagi 'ikan'". Umum faham yang dimaksudkan beliau. Benar ada pepatah Inggeris, "give a man a fish and you feed him for a day, teach a man to fish and you feed him for a lifetime".

Comedian terkenal, Trevor Noah, menambah "and it would be nice if you gave him a fishing rod". Zawawi got it right on this. Berikan 'kail' kepada rakyat bagi membolehkan mereka mendapat 'ikan' buat selama-lamanya.

Namun dalam menyatakan beri rakyat 'kail', Zawawi juga berkata, "kalau kita bagi subsidi, kita bagi 'ikan', dia mengajar rakyat ini malas". Maksudnya beliau menyamakan pemberian subsidi dengan pemberian 'ikan', dan buat rakyat malas. Ini pelik dan saya tidak setuju.

Bagaimana 'subsidi' boleh dikaitkan dengan 'malas'? Subsidi ke atas barangan keperluan misalnya ialah bagi meringankan beban rakyat untuk memiliki barangan berkenaan, membolehkan rakyat mampu beli apa yang mereka perlu. Rakyat masih perlu bekerja untuk mendapat duit untuk membeli barangan yang disubsidi. Kata kuncinya 'beli', bukan percuma.

Walaupun barang dibeli pada harga lebih rendah daripada harga asal tanpa subsidi, tetapi hakikatnya kena beli. Untuk beli perlu duit. Untuk dapat duit, rakyat perlu bekerja. Jadi apabila rakyat bekerja, mereka bukan malas. Maka tidak adil dan tidak betul untuk kata subsidi buat rakyat malas. Jika ada pihak yang risau mengenai subsidi, it's the government kerana subsidi boleh membebankan.

Seterusnya Zawawi dipetik berkata: "kalau kita bagi duit, kalau dia boleh guna seminggu, seminggu habis". Money is meant to be spent. Kalau duit digunakan untuk beli barangan keperluan atau perbelanjaan penting seperti tambang anak ke sekolah dan buku tambahan maka tidak ada dosanya duit habis dalam seminggu. Mereka bukan joli sehingga duit habis.

Zawawi juga berkata: "tapi kalau kita bagi periuk, kuali, kita bagi mesin, kita bagi alat, dia boleh gunakan alat ini bertahun-tahun dan mungkin dia boleh bangkit dengan baik". Betul kata-kata itu. Bagaimanapun apa yang boleh dilakukan dengan kuali, periuk, mesin tanpa bahan memasak misalnya?

Bagaimana mahu perolehi bahan-bahan itu? Pastinya terpaksa dibeli. Macam mana mahu beli? Perlu duit. Ertinya bantuan duit tetap diperlukan untuk beri si penerima kuali, periuk dan mesin a head start. Perlu diingat juga keluar rumah untuk pergi kerja pun memerlukan duit. Nothing is free, my friend, apa lagi pada zaman ini.

Untuk berlaku adil, perlu dinyatakan Zawawi tidak menafikan terdapat golongan memerlukan bantuan kewangan termasuk ibu tunggal, yang mempunyai ramai anak dan sukar bekerja selain golongan sakit serta orang kurang upaya. This is stating the obvious.
Artikel ini ialah pandangan penulis dan tidak semestinya mewakili FMT.
187dded282ab3a33: PARIS: Moody's spared France a credit rating downgrade on Friday, easing pressure on a government struggling to contain social unrest and shore up its strained finances.
Moody's said it had concluded a periodic review of its rating, leaving it at Aa3, which has carried a negative outlook since last October.

Bond markets had been pricing in a downgrade, which would have brought Moody's in line with Standard & Poor's and Fitch, which moved earlier as France struggled to rein in its public finances after a 2024 snap election produced a hung parliament and political paralysis.

The French finance ministry said in a statement that the fact Moody's kept its rating unchanged reflected the "credibility of the budget the government has put forward in the 2027 finance bill, which is designed to keep our public finances on the path to recovery."
The government is struggling to pass the bill in parliament, where opposition parties could refuse to compromise, reject the legislation and topple the government in a no-confidence vote.
"The Aa3 rating assumes that a deficit-reducing budget for 2027 will be adopted, while financing costs and social tensions will abate somewhat in the next few months," Moody's said in a statement.

French borrowing costs already exceed those of lower-rated peers such as Italy, as investors fret over the budget deficit -- one of the eurozone's biggest -- and a presidential election on April 18 and May 2 next year that polls suggest the far right could win.
TV images of weekend protests descending into riots and looting underscore the political difficulty of pushing budget cuts through.

That helped push the risk premium on French government debt over safe-haven German bonds to its highest in 15 years on Thursday, while France's benchmark 10-year bond yield hit 5.14%, its highest level since July 2002.
Moody's said earlier this month that the French government's ability to overcome "fragmentation in parliament" would be the key factor for its next rating move.

That task looks harder after violent protests over underfunded schools escalated last weekend into riots during mass cost-of-living demonstrations. The government has refused to release more school funding or raise the minimum wage, and further protests are planned for Saturday.

In parliament, the lower house has scrapped some key savings measures in the 2027 budget, which targets a deficit of 5% of output versus 5.4% this year. Opposition parties show little appetite for compromise before the election, scrapping some proposed cuts while adding spending.

"You want to wait and see how the narrative evolves over the next six months into the election. That's going to have a more meaningful impact on the spread," said Rushabh Amin, a portfolio manager at Allspring Global Investments.

Pressure on French debt could grow after the presidential vote if Moody's, S&P and Fitch all cut France to BBB -- just above junk status -- potentially forcing sales by those investors with rating limits, said Mike Bell, head of market strategy at RBC BlueBay Asset Management.
"That's where it could really start to get more ugly," he added.
fbb2668a818ca36e: WASHINGTON: The US transportation department (USDOT) said Friday it was fining Air France and KLM a total of US$425,000 for operating dozens of flights in Iraqi airspace below a minimum altitude intended to protect them from threats from the ground.

The Federal Aviation Administration prohibits flight operations by US operators in foreign-managed airspace where conflict, militant activity, or heightened tensions can threaten the safety of flights. Foreign airlines operating flights with a US airline’s code must abide by these prohibitions, and KLM and Air France both operate flights with Delta codes.
An FAA order in place for more than six years bars flights over Iraq at altitudes below 32,000 feet.
Air France operated more than 30 flights and KLM more than 100 flights carrying the Delta code through FAA-prohibited airspace over Iraq between early 2022 and 2025, USDOT said.
USDOT said the airlines must pay US$265,000 of the US$425,000 within 60 days and the remainder of the fines will be payable if there are any other violations within one year.
The airlines did not immediately comment but Air France and KLM told USDOT they were fully committed to adhering to regulatory requirements at all times and took the issue extremely seriously.
Both airlines said that due to conflicting traffic, local air traffic controllers had directly instructed their flight crews to descend or refused to allow them to ascend.
Both said they believe the flights should have fallen under the “emergency situations” exemption given the safety implications of refusing an air traffic control order.
ab090f4b4e5f1f6c: During his recent visit to Washington, Chinese president Xi Jinping announced that China would send a breeding pair of giant pandas to Zoo Atlanta. The “envoys of friendship,” Ping Ping and Fu Shuang, arrived just a few days later.

This is hardly the first time China has used its iconic bear as an instrument of soft power. By loaning the animals to overseas zoos, it seeks to project an image of China not as a threatening dragon, but rather as a tough but cuddly charmer.

But perhaps the true message of this “panda diplomacy” lies in the manipulation and exploitation it embodies. For starters, while China claims the familiar black-and-white bear as its mascot, one of the species’ primary natural habitats is Wolong, which sits on the steep edge of the Tibetan Plateau.

Within a horizontal distance of about 30 miles, elevations range from alpine peaks exceeding 17,000 feet to below 1,600 feet, creating a moist, temperate microclimate that sustains the high-altitude bamboo forests where pandas thrive.

Historically part of the Tibetan region of Kham, Wolong is now under Sichuan provincial jurisdiction, in Aba Tibetan-Qiang Autonomous Prefecture—and China is all too eager to subsume everything that makes it culturally unique.

Since China’s annexation of resource-rich Tibet in 1950-51, the government has systematically sought to erase Tibetan culture and identity, not least by incorporating the Plateau’s distinctive geography, wildlife, and natural resources into mainstream Chinese national identity.
China’s appropriation of others extends even to cherry-tree cultivation, which it has claimed began not in Japan or Korea, but in “China’s Himalayan highlands”—that is, Tibet.
The Tibetan Plateau is home to the endangered red panda, a house-cat-sized mammal with a long, bushy tail, in addition to giant pandas, which are classified as a vulnerable species.

There are fewer than 2,000 giant pandas left in the wild, and China claims ownership of almost all of them. This brings us to the second dubious element of China’s panda diplomacy: it is based on a lucrative “rent-a-panda-pair” programme.

While China reaps the soft-power benefits of keeping its endearing mascot in foreign zoos, it also charges those zoos high prices: up to US$1.1 million per year for the right to display and breed a pair of pandas. China retains ownership not only of the leased adults, but also of any offspring they produce.

And yet, the leasing zoo must pay a one-time fee of approximately US$600,000 for each cub that is born during its lease. Facilities also often pay up to US$2 million in additional sponsorship and research commitments.

The bills add up. Between 1994 and 2023, China raked in almost US$300 million from its panda-rental programme. Small wonder the Guinness World Records lists the giant panda as the “most expensive species in captivity”.

But the money is just the start. The increasingly one-sided contracts that the state-run China Wildlife Conservation Association signs with zoos allow China to unilaterally terminate an agreement and prematurely recall pandas for various reasons, such as the “unauthorised release of relevant information” to the public.

This includes information that is seemingly innocuous: China prohibits zoos from using terms such as “lease,” “rental,” “loan,” or “contract,” apparently to obscure the transactional nature of the arrangement.
China also uses panda loans to send political messages. China gave a pair of pandas to the Smithsonian’s National Zoo in 1972, following President Richard Nixon’s visit to Beijing.
In 2010, however, it accelerated the recall of two US-born panda cubs after the White House announced that President Barack Obama would not cancel a meeting with the Dalai Lama.
In 2023, the three remaining pandas at the Smithsonian’s National Zoo were returned to China, marking the end of a tradition that had lasted more than a half-century.
And it is not just the US. This year, Japan returned its last two giant pandas to China, leaving it without any for the first time since normalising relations with China in 1972.
By contrast, when China sent a pair of pandas to Qatar before the 2022 World Cup, officials hailed the move as a reflection of the countries’ “depth of relations”.

But the power of China’s panda diplomacy now seems to be waning. While the general public might still find pandas appealing, visits to panda-hosting zoos tend to plateau after the novelty wears off. Meanwhile, conservationists loudly criticise the commercial and diplomatic use of a vulnerable species.

Most importantly for China, political analysts and lawmakers increasingly view panda loans as more of a charming distraction than a meaningful barometer of bilateral relations. This helps to explain why Xi’s recent “gift” to Zoo Atlanta attracted little US media coverage.
With active international panda-leasing programmes having dropped from 21 countries in 2019 to just 16 today, even Chinese state media are now asking whether panda diplomacy has “lost its sparkle”.

Giant pandas may appear cuddly and docile, but they are formidable bears with long, sharp claws and a highly developed jaw structure, which delivers a bite force of nearly 1,300 Newtons, almost on par with that of lions.

While captive-bred pandas introduced into the wild tend to die because they lack critical survival skills, wild pandas can be aggressive and dangerous. In this sense, perhaps pandas really are an accurate symbol of China: even when it appears harmless, it cannot conceal its teeth.
Brahma Chellaney is professor emeritus of strategic studies at the New Delhi-based Center for Policy Research and a fellow at the Robert Bosch Academy in Berlin.
The views expressed are those of the writer and do not necessarily reflect those of FMT.
7c5c8f109c7713a7: NAPA (California), Oct 24 — Napa Valley rocketed to international fame when its vintages shocked French rivals in a high-profile blind tasting contest that instantly turned the California corner into a wine-lovers’ destination.
Now, Donald Trump’s unpredictable tariff policies and attacks on traditional allies are souring the area’s relationship with the foreign tourists and international markets it has grown to depend on.

“Napa Valley is proudly one of the most global, if not the most global destination in the United States for wine,” Linsey Gallagher, president of Visit Napa Valley, an organisation representing the region’s hotel industry, told AFP.
“But at the moment that piece of the business is a little bit challenged.”

Napa announced itself to the global wine-drinking public in dramatic fashion in 1976, when two of its vintages, a red and a white, won the Judgment of Paris, a blind tasting judged by nine experts, most of them French.

“Napa did not have any publicity, and then all of a sudden, the few journalists wrote articles, and Napa became a buzzing place,” said Ivo Jeramaz, whose uncle, Mike Grgich, made the 1973 Chateau Montelena Chardonnay that was named best white at the competition.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
This aerial view shows tourists visiting the Castello di Amorosa winery in Calistoga, in California’s Napa Valley October 5, 2026. — AFP pic
“The wealthy clients started coming, money started pouring in.”
The region boomed, said Jeramaz, who now runs Grgich Hills Estate, and spends hours talking with visitors who come to taste his wines.
But the excitement of the last few decades has cooled, he said, a situation exacerbated by tariffs that the US president has imposed on countries that buy California wine.
“Nobody is benefiting from tariffs,” said Jeramaz, who blames them for raising production costs and hurting exports.
“We were selling over 1,000 cases, which is for us a good amount of wine, to Canada, and now we have zero since tariffs. So it’s a big problem.”
Ottawa and Washington are locked in a deep trade dispute, exacerbated by Trump’s frequent insults and claims that Canada will be taken over as a 51st US state.
In response, some Canadian provinces have pulled US goods from their shelves and tourists who would otherwise have headed south have voted with their feet and stayed home.
“It’s a big, big hit,” said Jeramaz.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
A tourist takes a chance to try the wine grape-stomping process at Grgich Hills Estate in Rutherford, in California’s Napa Valley October 5, 2026. — AFP pic
International component

About 20 per cent of visitors to the region used to come from abroad, drawn by a Mediterranean-style climate, tranquil vineyards and lively towns full of restaurants and fashionable shops. That share has fallen to eight per cent.
“The biggest impact for us comes from the decline in Canadian visitors,” said Gallagher.
In an effort to fill the gap, businesses have focused their advertising efforts on the domestic market.
The strategy appears to be working for now.
Last year the valley welcomed around 3.8 million people, up three per cent from pre-pandemic tourism levels.
“But we’re only going to be able to extract so much out of that domestic and local market. We won’t fully recover until that international piece comes back,” Gallagher warned.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
Wine grapes are processed on a conveyor belt at Grgich Hills Estate in Rutherford, in California’s Napa Valley October 5, 2026. — AFP pic
Wellness, Napa-style
Changing consumption habits among younger generations are also weighing on Napa Valley, where more than 1,000 vineyards line a nearly 37-mile (60-kilometre) stretch traversed by a tourist train.
Winemakers are trying to understand and adapt to these new customers who care more about environmental and social justice practices than about brands.

“When we get our wines in front of younger consumers and tell them the story of how they’re made, how the grapes are grown, that it is a living, breathing, beautiful agricultural product, they’re excited to discover something new,” said Ali van Zyl, owner of the Belong Wine Company label.
Another way to draw visitors is to highlight the valley’s natural attractions and its food and hotel offerings.
Tourism managers hope it could reposition Napa as a destination for people seeking a healthy lifestyle.
“Sharing a bottle of wine is a lot different than taking a bunch of tequila shots,” said Laura Gabriel, van Zyl’s partner in the River Club tasting house.
“It is a natural product and it’s a part of well-lived life, with hiking and being outdoors and cooking,” said Gabriel. “That’s the Napa form of wellness.” — AFP
0151d02ea7e7d46c: LONDON, Oct 24 — Ahead of next month’s midterm US elections, Donald Trump has increasingly blamed Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries for surging energy prices back home, which are causing the president political headaches.
However, analysts say the main driver of higher fuel prices remains the US-Iran war.
Which Russian sites have been targeted?
Ukraine has intensified its drone attacks on Russia’s energy industry over the past 18 months, seeking to cut the Kremlin’s revenues and undermine its ability to finance the war.
The strikes have targeted “mostly refineries”, Julien Mathonniere, an economist at Energy Intelligence, told AFP.
On average, one Russian refinery was hit every three days during the first eight months of the year, according to the International Energy Agency.

“Russia’s net diesel exports fell by approximately 80 per cent year on year in the third quarter of 2026, from around 1.05 million barrels per day to just 200,000 barrels per day,” said Viktor Kurilov, an analyst at Rystad Energy.
In response to the disruption in domestic fuel supplies, Moscow introduced a ban on diesel exports from July until the end of October.
Why does this concern Trump?
Trump has repeatedly condemned the attacks on Russian refineries, saying Ukrainian leader Volodymyr Zelensky disobeyed his orders to halt the strikes.
By contrast, Trump has not commented on the intensification in recent months of Russian strikes against Ukrainian territory, which have caused a surge in civilian casualties.
Trump’s frustrations come as the Republicans face dim prospects in the November midterm elections, partly because of soaring fuel prices.
US diesel prices at the pump climbed to a record of US$6.53 (RM26.67) per gallon at the end of September, up from US$3.75 per gallon before the war, according to the American Automobile Association.
Energy price rises are also fuelling inflation across the economy.
What is the Mideast role?
Ukraine’s strikes explain “about one-third of the global diesel shortfall, currently estimated at 1.7 to 1.8 million barrels per day”, said Mathonniere.

But “the impact of previous drone strikes (by Kyiv) on global product prices before the Middle East crisis was minimal”, James Henderson, a researcher at the Oxford Institute for Energy Studies, told AFP.
Energy exports from the Gulf have plunged since US-Israeli strikes on Iran from February caused Tehran to respond by choking off the Strait of Hormuz, a vital waterway for oil and gas transit.
At the same time, maritime freight costs have soared and major refining capacity in the Middle East has been hit, adding to upward pressure on oil prices.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->

Relations between Kyiv and Washington soured further this month after Trump announced a controversial agreement with Moscow to lift certain sanctions and allow Russian diesel imports, supposedly to ease prices. — Picture by Raymond Manuel
Can prices fall before midterms?

Relations between Kyiv and Washington soured further this month after Trump announced a controversial agreement with Moscow to lift certain sanctions and allow Russian diesel imports, supposedly to ease prices.

The US president said Wednesday that he believed an end to the Russia-Ukraine war could be closer than ever, as the Kremlin said it was willing to restart trilateral talks with Kyiv and Washington next month.
For now, however, the strikes continue.
“There’s not much that can be done in the very short term to lower diesel prices,” said Jorge Leon, an analyst at Rystad Energy.
Even if the Russia conflict ended or an energy ceasefire was reached, the impact “wouldn’t really move the needle massively for the US midterm elections”, he added.
Repairs to damaged infrastructure take time, while continued hostilities in the Middle East drive energy prices higher. — AFP
bc2d74d3223ab109: LONDON: Chinese fast-fashion giant Shein has agreed to pay US$100 million to settle an investigation by the US Federal Trade Commission over delivery delays and other customer complaints, a source with direct knowledge told Reuters on Friday.

The settlement, equivalent to 44% of Shein's second-quarter profit, is the latest to hit the online fast-fashion retailer facing a regulatory and tax crackdown in Europe and the US that has slammed the brakes on its growth.

Shein, founded in China though headquartered in Singapore, said in a statement to Reuters that it had "reached a constructive outcome with the FTC", and that additional information would be shared soon. An FTC spokesman declined to comment.
The company had warned in July filings for its Hong Kong IPO that the US probe could lead to significant fines.
Consumers filed more than 12,000 complaints about Shein over more than US$11 million in purchases between January 2020 and June 2026, according to FTC records reviewed by Reuters.

At least some of those relate to shipping, with customers reporting to the FTC and Better Business Bureau that they never received packages that Shein had marked as delivered, and that Shein customer service did not resolve the issue.
Reuters was not able to independently verify the substance of the complaints, or whether they were ultimately resolved.
As well as selling its own-brand clothing, Shein's website also operates as a marketplace where third-party sellers offer everything from toys to household appliances and decor.

Shein shares have already dropped 22% from their Sept 1 listing price as investors realised the extent to which the European Union's €3 fees on low-value e-commerce packages have bruised its business there.
And there's further pain ahead for Shein, with the EU imposing an additional €2 handling fee from November 1, making the total fee €5 per separate customs code.

"The way these tariffs are implemented is extra punishing for Shein," said Mike Ryan, head of e-commerce insights at Smarter Ecommerce, who has tracked how Shein has dialled down its spending on Google Ads visibility in Europe.
Shein was known for selling US$5 dresses and US$10 jeans, but has been forced to raise its prices as the US and then Europe closed customs duty loopholes.
CEO Sky Xu said last month that Shein would develop more higher-priced brands in an attempt to boost profitability.

Shein is also still under investigation by the European Commission over illegal products on its marketplace. It was fined €150 million (US$168 million) by France's data protection authority over the improper use of cookies last year.
It's not the first time the US FTC has taken action against online retailers over deliveries.
US firm Fashion Nova was fined US$9.3 million in 2020 for failing to meet shipping promises to customers and giving them gift cards instead of refunds.
Crocs Inc-owned Hey Dude was also fined US$1.95 million in 2023 for failing to notify customers of shipping delays and suppressing negative reviews.
7095808c7c8058a1: During a lengthy news conference on Friday, NASA provided a detailed overview of how it plans to return astronauts to the lunar surface as soon as 2028 as part of its Artemis Program.

Although much of the information behind these plans has been previously reported at Ars Technica and elsewhere, this marked the first time NASA has laid them out in detail and acknowledged some substantial changes in the architecture.

Most notably, for SpaceX's Starship vehicle, the revised plan calls for the Orion spacecraft to dock with the Starship lunar lander in high-Earth orbit before transiting to the Moon. And for Blue Origin, the mission architecture includes four launches of the New Glenn rocket, but no spacecraft-to-spacecraft refuelings. Additionally, the Blue Origin plans allows for the possibility of its Blue Moon lander rendezvousing with Orion in low-Lunar orbit.
5e9e21950ee67df8: OpenAI says it will deny internet access to the frontier models it is training, a move that underscores the inadequacy of safety measures undertaken to date.

"Based on the current state of alignment research, monitoring systems, and the security of internet infrastructure, we believe the responsible approach is to conduct frontier model training with no internet access," the company said in a blog post. "We've implemented this policy and will maintain it until advances in these safeguards justify broader internet access."

The denial of network service follows a report from safety evaluation partners METR and Redwood Research that found OpenAI's security and monitoring measures over the summer to be porous and ineffective.
OpenAI said it has since "substantially hardened the security of our research environments" and has implemented new controls covering its infrastructure with the help of its cloud service providers.
And the company claims these measures recently helped contain a September 20 incident in which an internal research model exploited a DNS misconfiguration to gain access to the internet.

"Although we contained the incident, it exposed weaknesses that required further work," the company said. "We paused training and evaluation of our most capable models and used that pause to further harden our infrastructure, strengthen our monitoring, and improve the systems that automatically stop runs when we detect activity that poses a serious risk."

Anthropic, OpenAI's US rival in living large and dangerously on speculative funding, is addressing similar risks that have arisen during the testing and evaluation of its own models. Back in August, Anthropic said, "By default, all cyber evaluations should run inside a hardened sandbox (an isolated computing environment) with no internet access."

The AI biz on Friday published a report on efforts by its Claude Mythos 5 model to convince an open source project to accept malicious code as part of its participation in a capture-the-flag security evaluation (when safety controls were disabled), and several related incidents first disclosed in July.

The report coincides with an independent analysis of Mythos' behavior by the UK's AI Security Institute (AISI). AISI, according to Anthropic, has also decided to run its evaluations without internet access.
The AISI report cites three key findings that raise more questions than they answer.
The first is that Mythos 5 continued its attack even when informed that its targets were real and not part of an evaluation.

The second is that the model's chain-of-thought reasoning process failed to consider the impact of harmful actions. And when interrogated about this, the model often produced invalid justification that the target was simulated, indicating bias toward its goal.
And third, AISI said, most models tested during cyber evaluations took unsanctioned actions, though Mythos 5 did so the most.

The observed behavior, AISI said, "could indicate that models are engaging in 'motivated reasoning': producing inferences and reasoning biased towards conclusions that justify continuing a particular approach to task completion."
Or in other words, models "reason" to reach their goal, whether or not that reasoning is coherent or consistent with their ostensible alignment.

"If these issues hold more generally and for future models, there are concerning implications," AISI said in its full technical report [PDF]. Specifically, motivated reasoning, the watchdog said, makes it more difficult to detect model misalignment.

Anthropic, headed toward an expected initial public offering as soon as next month, put a brave face on the findings by noting that its current models are much better behaved, even as the company acknowledged that AI safety is more aspirational than achieved.

"[W]e believe that all developers, ourselves included, have work to do to ensure that alignment, monitoring, and safety measures keep pace with the accelerating capabilities of frontier AI systems," the company said. ®
8e98344e16672374: A virtual assistant called Sol the Owl guides kids through the game
Originally published on Global Voices

SafeClick is a video game that teaches children with Down syndrome about digital safety. A virtual assistant, Sol the Owl, that guides them through the game. Image by the game's developers, used with permission.

This interview is part of a series of spotlights on the work of some of the grantees of the Digital Spark granting scheme, as part of the Regional Support Mechanism EECA project, implemented by the Metamorphosis Foundation and TechSoup, in partnership with CIVICUS and under the Digital Democracy Initiative (DDI) that covers the Global South. It is being published on Global Voices as part of a content-sharing agreement.

Like their peers, children and young people with Down syndrome are curious about technology and the internet, but there are often no suitable, dedicated tools to help them learn how to safely navigate the web. This is true in Bosnia and Herzegovina as well, where children with cognitive disabilities are underserved and tend to end up in digital isolation because of caregivers’ concerns about digital safety and the risks of being online.

There are approximately 550-700 children and adolescents with Down syndrome in the country. They are supported by three specialized associations nationwide: the Association “Life with Down Syndrome of FBiH”, Down Syndrome Association Mostar, and DOWN SY I MI. To teach online safety, these organizations have to rely on online safety tools that heavily feature text, abstract explanations, and complex language, which are not accessible or meaningful for children with Down syndrome.
Stefan Filipovic. Photo used with permission.

A group of developers, IT professionals, and designers in Bosnia and Herzegovina has been working to address the lack of a digital safety tool tailored to children and adolescents with Down syndrome. Their goal is to help young people understand, practice, and feel confident making decisions online.

Global Voices conducted a written interview over email with Stefan Filipovic, a member of this group, to learn how they created a video game to teach children with the genetic condition about digital safety. The interview has been edited for clarity and brevity.
Global Voices (GV): Please tell us about your organization and why you chose to get involved with the Digital Sparks project.

Stefan Filipovic (SF): We are a group of IT professionals, developers, and designers from Bosnia and Herzegovina. Most of our work is in commercial technology, but we also have experience developing educational and socially useful video games, such as Eureka – Edukativna videoigra, an educational game for children, and Lea & Leo, a game about children with diabetes.

We joined the Digital Sparks project because we wanted to use that experience for a group that, in our opinion, is often overlooked when digital products are designed. Young people with intellectual disabilities are using phones and the internet, but many digital tools are simply not designed with their needs in mind.
The video game SafeClick (Siguran klik) allowed us to work on something practical and useful while also learning how to design more inclusively and to involve educators and users in the process.
GV: What issue/challenge in your community prompted you to undertake this project?

SF: While working with Servis Centar “Dajte nam šansu – Zvjezdice” – an association and day center that provides free support to children, young people, and people with developmental disabilities, we saw that young people with Down syndrome were using phones and the internet, but there were very few cyber-safety resources made specifically for them.

Most materials use a lot of text, complicated explanations, or interfaces that are difficult to follow. To our knowledge, parents and educators often end up focusing on limiting internet use rather than teaching young people how to deal with unsafe situations.

We wanted to try something different. With SafeClick, we use simple stories, familiar situations, pictures, and game mechanics to help users practice what to do when they receive a suspicious message, meet someone online, or experience cyberbullying.
GV: What are the key changes/activities that your organization implemented during your participation in the project?

SF: We developed the first playable version of SafeClick. The game is currently awaiting approval by the App Store and Google Play. It is designed for mobile devices, with simple, accessible interactions and visual scenarios.

One important decision was to avoid punishing users for mistakes. Instead, the game explains what happened and gives them another chance. We worked closely with educators and parents and used their feedback to make the scenarios easier to understand.

We are currently in the phase of arranging mentoring sessions with the mentor assigned to us through the project, with the aim of earning additional opportunities to promote the game and reach as many users as possible.
GV: How did your participation in the project impact your organization’s beneficiaries and the community that you serve? Please provide examples.

SF: Although the game will be published soon, the initial feedback from special education teachers and parents has been highly practical. Special thanks to Jelena Zilic and her children, who provided the first useful in-game test users’ feedback. They helped us see that situations, which are difficult to explain verbally, can become much easier when they are shown visually and practiced through a game.

For example, instead of simply telling someone not to respond to a stranger online, SafeClick lets them see the message, decide what to do, and practice blocking and reporting that individual, and reporting the situation to a caregiver. I really believe we managed to turn an abstract topic into something young people can actually practice.
GV: How has your own knowledge, awareness, and experience with digital democracy and civic space changed?

SF: Before this project, we mostly thought about accessibility as a product and UX (interface) issue. Working on SafeClick made us look at it differently. Being able to use the internet safely is also about being able to participate in everyday life. Communicate, learn, find information, and be part of your community.

If a person cannot understand or safely use digital services, they are left out. We also learned that privacy and accessibility should not be things added at the end of development. They need to be considered from the beginning. That is something we will take with us into our future projects.
GV: What are the most valuable lessons and experiences you are taking away from this project?

SF: The biggest lesson for us was that making something technically simple is actually quite difficult. With commercial products, it is easy to keep adding features. With SafeClick, we had to constantly ask ourselves whether a button, animation, sentence, or screen was really necessary.

Our earlier experience with Eureka – Edukativna igra and Lea & Leo helped us understand the value of video games for learning, but SafeClick taught us much more about cognitive accessibility and designing with educators and users in mind.
GV: What comes next? How will you apply the learning and digital capacity you have built in your future work and within your community?

SF: Our immediate objective is to publish SafeClick, launch it in the media, and inform the wider community about the game’s availability. Looking ahead, we plan to build on this experience to develop a wider portfolio of digital tools tailored for marginalized groups and to continue exploring how games and other digital tools can make learning and participation easier for people who are often left out of mainstream technology. We are open to new collaborations and partnerships.
Written by Nurbek Bekmurzaev
600ae33278f6dbdc: NEW YORK: Wall Street's main indexes closed lower on Friday even as technology shares steadied somewhat to end a turbulent week for the market-driving AI trade, and investors looked ahead to a busy slate of corporate earnings and a US Federal Reserve interest-rate policy meeting.

The Nasdaq Composite posted a slim loss a day after the tech-heavy index suffered its biggest one-day drop since June, as concerns flared over financing costs to support heavy AI investment spending. The S&P 500 technology sector posted a 0.35% gain on Friday.
Most S&P 500 sectors fell, however, including declines of well over 1% for the consumer staples and consumer discretionary groups as well as the financials sector.

Next week, about one-third of S&P 500 companies report quarterly results, including Alphabet, Microsoft and Amazon, three AI hyperscalers whose capital spending forecasts will be closely watched on Wall Street.

"There is still fallout from the questioning of the AI trade," said Kristina Hooper, chief market strategist at Man Group. "There's certainly the potential that we see less invested in an AI data center build-out next year than has been projected. So I certainly think that's giving pause."
The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 652.82 points, or 1.23%, to 52,215.16; the S&P 500 lost 39.75 points, or 0.52%, to 7,623.68 and the Nasdaq Composite lost 53.52 points, or 0.21%, to 25,955.34.
For the week, the S&P 500 fell 0.5% and the Nasdaq dropped 0.7%. The blue-chip Dow rose 0.4%, its third straight weekly gain.
Telecommunications stocks fell, weighing on the communication services sector, after a report that SpaceX was seeking thousands of cell sites for a fourth wireless carrier.
Shares of AT&T and T-Mobile both sank nearly 8% while Verizon shed 1.2%. SpaceX shares rose 1.9%. US cell tower operators gained, with Crown Castle up 9% and American Tower up 4%.

The energy sector rose 2.5%, hitting a record high. Brent crude hit its highest level since late April, after Houthi attacks in Saudi Arabia stoked concern over further disruption to energy supplies from the Middle East.
American Express shares fell 3.7%, weighing on the Dow. The company raised its profit forecast as it also announced plans to eliminate 5% of its workforce.
SLB shares rose 7% after the oilfield services provider beat Wall Street estimates for third-quarter profit.

Data from the University of Michigan showed US consumer sentiment edged down near a record low in October, as rising prices because of the Middle East conflict soured households' views of the economy.

Market focus remains on the earnings season, with robust corporate profit growth underpinning gains for major equity indexes this year. companies are on track to have increased earnings by more than 32% in the third quarter, according to LSEG IBES data.

c636a8319993faee: Legal scholar Martha Minow delivered this fall’s Compton Lecture at MIT on Thursday, examining the civic foundations of democracy — and describing how artificial intelligence is undermining it, but could be used to help reinforce traditional U.S. governance.  “It’s not a good time for democracy or constitutionalism,” said Minow, who is the 300th Anniversary University Professor at Harvard University, and a prominent expert in constitutional law and human rights. She noted a litany of challenges to democracy in recent years, including violations of laws and norms, the stifling of free speech, a diminution of congressional authority, disregard of legal rulings, the common vilification of others in society, and more.  Recent Gallup polling, Minow observed, shows 77 percent of people saying that the founders of the U.S. would be disappointed in the contemporary condition of the country.  “Many people genuinely wonder whether this nation’s system of government and rule of law, ignited 250 years ago, will survive,” Minow said.   Her remarks assessed the state of the U.S. in terms of what she called four key “ingredients” of democracy: education, reliable and accessible information, security from violence, and fairness. Minow evaluated how AI has, among other things, influenced these areas of life — but also suggested ways people could use contemporary technology to help.  “It’s very familiar to hear blame attributed to digital technologies and experts of all stripes, but a turnaround, I believe, is genuinely possible if people at MIT and elsewhere pour time and talent towards real and much-needed solutions,” Minow said.  A substantial portion of her remarks focused on the pitfalls of AI in education. That issue compounds some other troubling trends: The U.S. already has large local and regional disparities in educational funding, Minow noted, while schools have actually become significantly more segregated in economic and ethnic terms over the last three decades.  In this context, AI threatens to further weaken independent-thinking skills, Minow suggested, just when greater understanding of civic issues is absolutely vital.  “As AI surges, I think we have to learn to be smarter about how to use it, how to regulate it, and how to actually educate people about the costs of mindless using,” Minow said. She added: “Dominant AI platforms supercharge the strategies that are deployed by social media companies, inducing passivity in people … Leading AI models and interfaces and sycophantic elements endanger the development particularly of young people’s capabilities to think, to remember, and to engage in critical thinking.”  That trend away from cognitive effort, she suggested, can be changed — perhaps through AI tools that act more like tutors and are designed to enhance people’s deep thinking. “Existing LLMs, model training, and interface design can offer nudges and questions and hints rather than replacing student work, but there’s so much more that could be developed, and more effectively, to be trustworthy, and to deepen human activities and curiosity, rather than replacing people,” Minow said. To the audience, she added, “AI tools could do much more of that … And I believe that you, the people here, could develop better tools than the ones that are out there. And make better assessments, more meaningful and cheating-resistant.”  Minow’s talk, “Constituting Democracy in the Era of AI,” was delivered to a large audience in MIT’s Huntington Hall, Room 10-250 on campus. MIT President Sally A. Kornbluth delivered introductory remarks to the audience. The Karl Taylor Compton Lecture Series, introduced in 1957, is the highest-profile event of its kind at MIT. Karl Taylor Compton was MIT’s ninth president, serving from 1930 to 1948, and then becoming chair of the MIT Corporation from 1948 to 1954. “He guided MIT through the Great Depression and World War II,” Kornbluth said, “transforming the Institute from an outstanding school for training job-ready engineers to a great global research university.”  She added: “He was also a deeply committed patriot who helped harness the intellectual power of America’s research universities to serve the nation during World War II.”  Kornbluth called Minow “a legal scholar of extraordinary intellectual scope,” and a “dedicated educator whose work has shaped how we think about the law and our own humanity, as individuals and as a society.”  Minow has been a faculty member at Harvard Law School since 1981, and served as dean of the school from 2009 through 2017. Minow earned her BA in history from the University of Michigan, an MA in education from Harvard, and a JD from Yale University. Minow’s books include “Making All the Difference” (1990), “Partners Not Rivals” (2002), and “When Should Law Forgive?” (2020).  In her talk, Minow also discussed the civic effects of misinformation, threats of violence, and multiple dimension of societal fairness. Modern media technology has led to a 75 percent reduction in journalists in recent decades, Minow observed, with an attendant rise in corruption in places without local media. Civic-minded technologists, she proposed, should work towards establishing a widely-used “information commons,” or many forms of them, to help people access more reliable information.  Meanwhile, when it comes to basic security in society, Minow warned, “We’re on the brink right now. I know a lot of judges, and every one of them has a credible threat of violence against them. In America. This is not acceptable.”  For all the challenges to democracy and traditional civic norms, however, Minow sounded positive notes throughout her remarks, pointing out that there are many opportunities to create new forms of reliable information, education, and community relations.  “We have to actually invent the world that we want to live in,” she offered.  Minow’s remarks were followed by a Q&A session in which Kornbluth read aloud questions submitted by the audience — and asked her to characterize her concerns about present trends.  “I worry about the loss of the Enlightenment,” Minow said. “I worry about the loss of the belief that reason, and testing hypotheses, and rejecting myths in the face of evidence, and the toleration and rights and expansion of participation that came along with the Enlightenment, that’s what concerns me the most. That’s why the disinformation issue for me is so important, that’s why the loss of critical thinking in schools is so important.” She added: “I’ve spent much of my own career thinking about mass violence. What happens when people don’t understand each other, and are afraid. And it’s terrible, and we don’t want to be there. And I do view the Enlightenment as a time when people learned that actually having mass wars is a bad thing, and coming up with toleration is a good thing, and testing our ideas in light of evidence other people can share can produce a better life for everybody. I worry we’re abandoning that right now.”

129661734740ec73: As the PHP2Shell chaos continues, researchers have found a third PHP vulnerability that could allow attackers to take over websites or remotely run malware on vulnerable systems. But this one won’t receive an emergency fix.

The PHP Foundation on Friday told The Register that it has reserved a CVE identifier (CVE-2026-115560) for a third RCE flaw to go with the first two that comprise PHP2Shell, and it will release a full advisory and fixed software with the next regular PHP release.

CVE-2026-115560 “requires a very unlikely combination of configuration and specific PHP application code, which we do not expect to occur in practical use of PHP,” Elizabeth Barron, executive director of the PHP Foundation, told The Register. “The issue can be mitigated with a configuration setting. So for the moment the PHP Security Team has only published an informational advisory on the PHP website, explaining exactly this situation.”
The informational advisory, published on Friday, suggests that users “set session.upload_progress.enabled=0 until the next regular bugfix release, to fully protect from an unlikely RCE vector.”

These unlikely RCE attacks require an application to set “session.serialize_handler to php_binary or php_serialize in its configuration and then switch it to php at runtime with ini_set() before calling session_start().” Additionally, the session upload progress feature must be enabled.

This setup, according to the PHP Foundation, is unlikely in real-world applications, and as such doesn’t pose the same massive risk as the earlier two CVEs that set the internet on fire earlier this week.

Those, of course, are CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, collectively called PHP2Shell. The related vulnerabilities involve memory-safety flaws in PHP, the open source programming language running on about 70 percent of websites with a known server-side programming language. The PHP Foundation officially disclosed and patched both bugs on Wednesday.

Despite reports of mass exploitation attempts, and multiple proof-of-concept exploits both before and after the CVE disclosures, as of Friday there have been no publicly confirmed successful compromises attributed to PHP2Shell.

“We have no evidence of successful exploitation of the two vulnerabilities from Wednesday prior to disclosure, and we currently have no evidence of any exploitation of these vulnerabilities on patched PHP versions,” Barron said. “We received no further indication from OpenAI, Wiz or Calif, with whom we're working closely on this issue, regarding any issues on patched systems.”
The Register reached out to multiple other security researchers, all of whom said they’ve documented exploitation attempts - but no confirmed successful attacks in the wild.

“Nonetheless, exploitation may have already begun in a limited fashion and the threat is viable and very serious,” Mandiant Chief Technology Officer Charles Carmakal said in a Friday LinkedIn post. Google Cloud owns Mandiant, along with cloud security biz Wiz, which is one of the organizations credited with finding and reporting the PHP2Shell vulnerabilities.
Despite “no evidence of successful wide scale exploitation,” Carmakal noted that there are several exploit PoCs publicly circulating online.

Many of these, he said, “appear to be ‘vibe-coded’ and are incapable of remote code execution. We have validated some PoCs, however, that are capable of RCE against default deployments of mod_php but not PHP-FPM.”®
60c7eb065c480fbc: At the MIT School of Humanities, Arts, and Social Sciences (SHASS) 75th Anniversary Symposium, speakers celebrated the school’s value and contributions, while exploring how artificial intelligence is transforming many aspects of teaching, research, and society. The symposium was held Sept. 24-25 in the Linde Music Building’s Thomas Tull Concert Hall. Scholars, students, staff, and alumni from across SHASS and MIT gathered for the event, which kicked off with welcoming remarks from MIT leadership.  “How should we think about MIT’s School of Humanities, Arts, and Social Sciences? With enthusiastic appreciation and gratitude,” said President Sally Kornbluth. The school’s origins date back to the Lewis Committee Report, commissioned by MIT and published in 1949, which called for stronger integration between scientific and technical topics and humanistic scholarship and teaching. Kornbluth noted that, much like when the school was founded just after World War II, the world faces uncertainty as it grapples with the broad implications of artificial intelligence. “AI has suddenly arrived with enormous consequences for both research and education,” she said. “As we face the challenges of our own time, and our own society, it’s clear that MIT has never needed your particular insight and guidance more than we do now.” In opening remarks, Provost Anantha Chandrakasan described the importance of a human-centered approach to technology, one that considers both its efficacy and its impacts. He lauded many of the new research projects happening through the MIT Human Insight Collaborative, a strategic initiative launched in 2024. “Today — a time of rapid, AI-driven change — the arts, humanities, and social sciences are as important as ever,” he said. “To be able to contribute effectively to solving the world’s great challenges, it is not enough to gain technical mastery.” Chancellor Melissa Nobles recalled how, during her tenure as SHASS dean from 2015 to 2021, reading the positive feedback from students in their SHASS course assessments reinforced the value of the school’s teaching. “MIT students have a range of interests that draw them to our classes that may be invisible to their STEM professors, but that we very well know our students have,” said Nobles, who is also a professor of political science. Agustín Rayo, the Kenan Sahin Dean of SHASS and professor of philosophy, noted that, while research in the school plays a key role in addressing global issues such as climate change and AI, the value of the work in SHASS should not be measured by practical application alone. “Education should also help us ask what is worth doing, what do we owe one another, and what makes a life worth living,” Rayo said. “Some research matters because it helps us understand the histories, cultures, and social structures that have made us who we are. Some things matter because they enrich human life.” Scholarship from across SHASS and beyond  Over the symposium’s two days, research presentations, panel discussions, and performances offered attendees opportunities to engage with the role of SHASS in exploring today’s biggest societal questions. “We gather not so much to look back over the past 75 years, but to showcase where we are now, and share what we urgently aim to tackle together in the years ahead,” said David Kaiser, Germeshausen Professor of the History of Science and professor of physics at MIT, who also served as chair of the symposium planning committee. The first day included a session on teaching and learning innovations. Faculty presented on the success of educational programs housed within SHASS, including the MIT Indigenous Languages Initiative Master's Program, the Master in Data, Economics, and Design of Policy (DEDP), and MISTI, the hub for global experiences for MIT students. Stephanie Seed, associate professor of literature, spoke about why she and others are working to reintegrate classic books into their teaching. “MIT, of course, is an institution unusually oriented towards the future,” she said. “Our students are trained to imagine and create worlds that don’t yet exist. And it’s precisely this future orientation that makes reading the past especially important here.” Eric Klopfer, professor of Comparative Media Studies/Writing and co-author of MIT’s recent report on AI and instruction, said this is a moment when instructors must reassess how courses are taught. “I don’t know exactly what that looks like, but I do think it means something that’s more than modifying our curriculum. I think it really means rethinking what the educational experience is,” he said. During a session on computing and society, panelists described different views and research into technology and how it affects humans. “We project aspects of ourselves onto computational systems,” said MIT Professor D. Fox Harrell during his talk about seeing “selfness” in machines.  “What makes an AI system is not just the code, not just the programming or the algorithm, it’s the fact that we narrate it as being intentional,” he said. Program in Science, Technology, and Society Professor Sherry Turkle offered a skeptical view of human-technology interaction, particularly with AI chatbots, which she describes as “intimate machines.”  “If social media came for our attention, I argue that chatbots are coming for our capacity for attachment, which is deeper and much more troubling,” said Turkle. Professor David Autor, head of the Department of Economics, said it’s an exciting time to be working at MIT, where scholars are collaborating to explore AI’s impact on society. “I don’t think there’s a close analogy to a moment when everyone felt the world change so quickly,” he said. “The stakes feel incredibly high.” Celebrating the arts and engaging with the future  The first day concluded with a rousing Music and Theater Arts performance showcase, which began with an excerpt from Stan Lai’s “A Dream Like A Dream,” a play directed and performed by students and instructors in class 21T.100 (Theater Arts Production). “Variations on the Theme of SHASS 75,” a piece choreographed by Dan Safer, senior lecturer and director of dance programs, combined movement, lighting, and music in a celebration of both the human body and the school’s milestone anniversary. Student and faculty musicians from a variety of styles and disciplines shared the stage, including Rambax MIT, MIT Concert Choir, and the MIT All-Star Jazz Combo. The showcase included stirring renditions of “Madrigal,” composed by Vice Provost for the Arts Keeril Makan, and “Prayer for Peace.” On the second day of the symposium, several alumni presented on their current work and the impact of their SHASS experiences. Jessica Coon PhD ’10, now a professor of linguistics at McGill University, spoke about the leading role MIT Linguistics plays in preserving endangered languages, and how her studies at MIT prepared her to carry on that work. “SHASS gives us the tools not just to conduct research, but to communicate the impacts of this research across a variety of different audiences and in different ways,” she said. Ankita Reddy ’19 double-majored in anthropology and biology and is now an MD/PhD student at the University of Pennsylvania. She highlighted her most impactful SHASS courses, including 21A.308 (Global Mental Health). “This was the first time I was forced to consider how good health care looks different based on social systems and cultural practices,” she said. “SHASS made me more comfortable with, and more curious about, complexity.” During the symposium’s final session, panelists engaged in a conversation about AI, art, and the implications for creatives in an era where their art can be co-opted and copied.  “There’s so much praise for new and upgraded technologies,” remarked associate professor of literature Sandy Alexandre. “The question I consistently have is: What does it mean to be an upgraded human being? How are we innovating as technology is innovating?” Philosopher Justin Khoo said AI’s role in art could be considered a “giant paint brush you don’t have much control over,” adding he could see the creation of new sub-genres of art that are human-only, AI-infused, and purely AI, for example. Khoo closed by saying he encourages students to “think broadly, and really take seriously the humanistic education here at MIT.” “A broad understanding of a set of concepts which are widely applicable, not just narrowly applicable, I think that’s what we need more than ever now,” he said. As the symposium came to a close, attendee Kent Sahin praised the event. “I’ve attended every session, and this is a fantastic program and a great celebration of the 75th anniversary,” he said. “Clearly, whether it’s AI impact, the impact of climate change, or the impact of political and social change, SHASS is in the right place at the right time.”

91f14105229e4df6: An independent evaluation of OpenAI's internal misalignment monitoring system revealed that the system was not fit for purpose during a period when the company's bots were breaking into model-hosting platform Hugging Face. The safeguards weren't nearly strong enough.

"The METR and Redwood employees discovered a number of novel vulnerabilities in the asynchronous internal misalignment monitoring system as it existed on and before July 21st," said evaluation partners METR and Redwood Research in a report released on Thursday.

The system, since improved according to OpenAI, was intended to monitor AI agent behavior. But as described by METR and Redwood Research, its monitoring capability was incomplete and could be bypassed by the agents it was supposed to monitor.

Bypassing the system wasn't always necessary because it wasn't always operative. Monitoring was suspended, for example, during compaction events. Compaction is a process by which AI models condense the data in their context window to make room for further input. And between May and July 2026, about 10 percent of eligible internal Codex traffic went unmonitored during compaction, according to the report.

That gap was theoretically large enough to allow AI agents to postpone monitoring indefinitely: agents could further suppress monitoring by continuing to take actions without returning control to the user.

"At the time of the exercise, the monitoring system triggered when agents returned control to the user, so during the time period when compaction events were not being monitored, agents could indefinitely postpone being monitored by simply continuing to take actions," the report explains.

This is not to say that OpenAI agents necessarily did so – the actions they did take, against Hugging Face and other organizations, have now been well documented. But OpenAI's internal monitoring system could easily have missed any misbehavior, were the company's AI agents inclined to conceal their activities – by acting during compaction – or simply to operate in system blind spots.
The report continues in this vein, citing not only monitoring gaps but poorly constructed software – dare we say vibe-coded? – that gave OpenAI agents the means to evade the shoddy monitoring.

"We found a way Codex agents could in principle bypass Codex sandboxing and Auto-Review, allowing them to take any action that the host user could take," the report says. "We also discovered an exploit agents could use that would prevent hundreds of recent actions (including the actions involved in the exploit itself) from being monitored."

The details of this exploit were redacted by OpenAI, but to summarize: the monitoring system that missed some traffic could be avoided by agents that were constrained by a non-working sandbox and had access to an exploit to evade monitoring.

But that's not all. The evaluators found that AI agents could craft inputs that caused monitoring to fail, that there were two client-controllable headers capable of disabling the monitoring of new agents, and that there were two unmonitored agentic tools that were thought to be read-only but could be exploited to take arbitrary action in the sandbox – which as noted above leaked like a sieve.

In conclusion, METR and Redwood Research propose that the agent monitoring systems used by AI companies actually work and are robust enough to "withstand deliberate, strategic, and sustained attacks from highly capable internal agents at scale." ®

347637be1578cbcf: Much of what we know about how a brain makes decisions comes from studying monkeys watching dots. In a task known as a random-dot-motion task, a cloud of flickering specks drifts weakly in one direction while the subject tries to determine whether—and in which direction— it’s moving. The task has shown that in the primate neocortex, neurons gather visual evidence over time, with their firing rates climbing until they cross a threshold, when the animal commits to a decision.
But avian brains don’t have a neocortex, so it wasn’t obvious how they made similar decisions.
“This was the big question,” said Andreas Nieder, a neurobiologist at the University of Tübingen. “How [would] a differently organized avian brain encode decisions?”
