TRANSCRIPT:
At The Money: Dividend Growth Investing with David Bahnsen
Part 2 — Bloomberg Radio

David Bahnsen is founder, managing partner and chief investment officer of The Bahnsen Group, a national private wealth management firm. His new book is Profit from the Profit: The Past, Present, and Future of Dividend Growth Investing.

BARRY RITHOLTZ: Dividends are one of the oldest and most highly regarded forms of equity investing. But in an era of mega-cap growth stocks, should you own dividend-paying equities? To help us unpack all of this and what it means for your portfolio, my extra special guest is David Bahnsen. He is the founder and chief investment officer of The Bahnsen Group and author of a brand-new book, Profit from the Profit: The Past, Present, and Future of Dividend Growth Investing. Welcome, David. Thank you so much for joining us.
DAVID BAHNSEN: Good to be with you, Barry.

BARRY RITHOLTZ: So let’s start with first principles. Given the current environment with AI and semiconductors and tech, which tend not to pay dividends, why should investors care about dividends when really it’s all about total return these days?

DAVID BAHNSEN: Well, I don’t think it’s ever a matter of dividends versus total return. It’s a way in which people get to total return. And I think that you bring up a great point: the big tech moment caused some people to believe they don’t need dividends, they don’t need value, they don’t need valuation. We think that the way the dot-com tech moment ended is somewhat of a rebuttal to that thinking. It didn’t end very well.

We are in a moment in this AI period where some of the largest free-cash-flow-generating companies in history are now negative free cash flow because the capex is so high. We don’t want to make a call on how that’s going to play out. We would just simply suggest that there’s a different risk profile when companies are returning capital from free cash flow to shareholders — still profitable, still growing profits, healthy balance sheets. And by the way, there are some great dividend growers even within the AI world. Our ownership of Broadcom over a seven-year period is one of the most profitable investments we ever had.

You can’t really have the AI moment without data centers. Blackstone is one of the great dividend growers of the last decade. So it just takes the research to go find the right names that fit into the narrative.

BARRY RITHOLTZ: So let’s stay with that point. What does it reveal about a company and its business when they’re willing to consistently pay a dividend, consistently increase that dividend? What does that tell us that sometimes earnings reports might not catch?

DAVID BAHNSEN: Well, dividends don’t lie. They’re cash. And it’s a line I’ve used many times over the last 25 years, Barry: there are plenty of people whose tax return shows an income that’s lower than what they really make. But there’s nobody whose tax return shows an income that’s higher than they really make. People don’t pay taxes on income they didn’t make. A dividend is real, and it reflects something real. In EBITDA you have a lot of opportunities for, let’s just say, not totally verifiable growth of a company. And so free cash flow is pure. A dividend from it reflects management’s confidence in the growth of the business. A slowing growth of the dividend maybe reflects management’s own view, but there’s nobody who should have a better view of things.
And you could trust their press releases if you want. You can trust the 10-Qs and what they say. But I really trust cash they put in my bank account.

BARRY RITHOLTZ: So let’s distinguish between companies, especially mature businesses, that continue to grow their dividends versus those companies that seem to be running out of ways to manage their cash.

DAVID BAHNSEN: Well, that’s a very important distinction, and it’s not just managing their cash, but it’s growing their business. Look, there’s no company that should never get to a point of cash flow productivity. When you are growing and you have infinite reinvestment opportunities where you’re getting a higher return on invested capital than the investor can get, you should be continuing to reinvest your own cash.

But eventually there is no infinity of what a company can do with that cash. So what do they end up doing when they don’t want to return it? They either just hold onto it and manage it in their own cash management vehicles — Apple’s been doing this forever. So do you want Apple holding on to hundreds of billions of cash in their own cash management vehicles? Or what do companies really end up doing most of the time? CEOs are notorious for M&A, and I would suggest that most M&A has served to be vanity projects and capital destructive. Now, not all — there are some that have been very synergistic. But when you look at the kind of return on equity that is generated from the great dividend growers over time, when they mature to a point that they can do it, their returns are unlike anything we’ve ever seen in history.

BARRY RITHOLTZ: So I’m glad you brought up Apple, which has become very well known for a massive stock buyback program over the past 10, 15 years. How do you compare the usage of free cash flow to either issue a dividend or to buy stock back? They’re both a return of capital to investors, but in a very different structure.

DAVID BAHNSEN: The problem, Barry, is that more often than not, they’re not a way to return capital to shareholders. How do you have record levels of share buybacks and yet more shares that exist now than did before all these share buybacks? The math is what it is. And so you have to look to net share issuance. And if they’re doing share buybacks, the net share issuance should be negative. But why has it grown leaps and bounds? Because for the most part — I’m not picking on Apple here or any particular company, but across the spectrum, and Silicon Valley’s notorious for this — share buybacks are executive compensation. They are not return of capital to shareholders.

Now, where companies are reducing their share count, that is a way to return capital to shareholders, and I’m all for it as a both/and. But my argument is that to the extent many investors are retirement oriented, they’re cash flow oriented, they need periodic income — you can’t eat a stock buyback. And so there is still something that is just tangible about receiving the cash of it. But the other issue is share buybacks go first whenever a company runs into trouble, and dividends tend to be last, because of that social contract that has been created by great dividend growers over long periods of time. So from the financial crisis of ’08 to the COVID moment, we saw this: share buybacks all but evaporated. For the great dividend growers — and I can speak to the portfolio we manage — we had zero dividend cuts through that horrible period. So it isn’t a hundred percent immune from the risk, but it’s far more immune from it than share buybacks.

BARRY RITHOLTZ: So I’m so glad you brought that up, because the question always comes up: when is a dividend sustainable? So what measures do you look at? Is it free cash flow or growth rate or earnings stability? Why not just buy the stocks with the highest dividend yield?

DAVID BAHNSEN: Well, the sustainability of the dividend is a very different question than why not buy the ones at the highest yield. Because the highest yield often could be a very imminent dividend cut — what I refer to as accidental high yielders. It’s just math, right? You have a 4% yield, a hundred-dollar stock price, you’re getting four bucks, and then the stock goes down to 50. You’re still getting four bucks, but now it’s 8%. Did you really get anything better? No. Did you lose 50% of your value? Yes. That’s not what we want. We want the yield going higher because the dividend’s going higher. And so there’s a big difference between a high yielder and a dividend grower.

Now, what do we look to? You mentioned three or four quantitative metrics. The answer is all of the above and then some. But where I just simply do not believe this can be done quantitatively, exclusively or passively, is in that qualitative element of when a company wants to pay the dividend, not when they’ve been dragged into doing it. So there is a cultural propensity to grow the dividend. Some C-suites do not like it, and we want to avoid those. Some where you have heavy founder ownership — I think of a company like Lamar Advertising or Enterprise Products Partners, which is still heavily owned by the family that started the company. They’re receiving just billions of dollars of dividends each year. They want to keep growing those dividends. So we like those stories where the alignment of management and shareholder is there.

BARRY RITHOLTZ: So you mentioned the stock that got cut in half, and it appears the dividend yield has doubled when in reality it’s four bucks either way. That’s a classic yield trap, a classic dividend trap. What are the warning signs investors should be aware of when, hey, this looks like it’s high yield, but really it’s a dividend cut waiting to happen?

DAVID BAHNSEN: Well, one of the issues I believe has been a career saver or career maker for me, Barry — you of course were a prolific writer at the time of the financial crisis — I sold Citigroup stock at $51 a share when they announced they weren’t cutting their dividend in October of 2007, and it went to 97 cents. And so I don’t want to confuse everyone if they’re looking at charts now; reverse stock splits have confused everything. But I’m talking in 2007 numbers. This stock really did go down 99%, as you know.

So why did I sell the stock at $51 and then spend the next few years bragging to clients that we did? Because they said, “We’re not cutting the dividend, but we just borrowed $10.5 billion from the Saudi Arabians and Kuwaitis” at, I think it was, a 10% coupon on the debt. Borrowing from your credit card to pay your bills is not how a dividend gets sustained, as you and I know. Citi was a great example. So you have to look to the qualitative realities of the business. And when a company’s at $4 and they’ve been growing it for 20 years and they stop growing it, but they haven’t cut it yet — that’s a warning sign. When the rate of growth slows, that’s a warning sign. So we look to the free cash flow, the business model, the competition that’s come in, the investment thesis. It requires fundamental research. It is true.

The Procter & Gambles, the Exxon Mobils, the McDonald’s, the Johnson & Johnsons — they’ve managed to a payout ratio, a balance sheet, a cash flow that’s enabled them to continue growing through thick and thin. Other companies are too tight; they’re paying out 90% already and there’s no margin for error. So we have to take that a little more seriously. But this is why I believe it requires some active management. We’ve done it well over the years. A lot of people that really are invested in this have done well with it, but it isn’t foolproof. General Electric cut their dividend. AT&T cut their dividend. But there were clear warning signs those were coming for those paying attention.

BARRY RITHOLTZ: So I like the example of Citigroup, and you and I can swap war stories over lunch. But you raise a really interesting question. A company consistently paying a dividend, if purchased at the wrong time — or even more importantly, the wrong price — can be a total disaster. How do you think about valuation and price when you’re making a purchase of a dividend stock?

DAVID BAHNSEN: Well, it’s interesting. A lot of people have a valuation metric, and valuation is very important to us, both for margin of safety but also just because we think total expected return is relevant to entry price. People with a calculator should be able to verify that I’m right about that. What you pay matters for your total expected return. So the P/E ratio is the most common, and people can use forward or backward. And people look at CAPE, and you can look at price to cash flow, you can look at price to book. I think all these valuation metrics matter. But why is dividend yield itself not a valuation metric — a company’s own historical dividend yield? So there are companies we own right now that have a 2% dividend yield, and they’ve been growing it like crazy, and yet they’ve historically had a three-and-a-half percent dividend yield. It’s just that the stock price is so high.

It pained me, Barry, to sell Walmart about a year and a half ago. I’d owned it my whole career. We made a fortune. Walmart went public the year before I was born and grew the dividend every year of my life. They didn’t do anything wrong. They just happened to go up 60% in one year in stock price. And what had been a three-and-a-half percent dividend yield on average for decades was now one and a half percent — basically an S&P 500-level yield. So from a valuation metric, we sold the stock. Same with Broadcom. The stock was up 16 times. They had grown the dividend 14% per year for eight years in a row. But the yield got to be 1%. So we used the yield as a valuation metric itself.

BARRY RITHOLTZ: So we’re recording this the day the book comes out, August 25th, 2026. And this is an era of relatively sticky inflation. We’ve seen 10-year rates and yields come up to almost 5%. We haven’t had a recession in a while, and we certainly haven’t had a major bear market in a while. But I’m curious, how do dividend-yielding stocks and how do dividend growth stocks do in the sort of environment of rising interest rates and high inflation? How do they do during recessions and bear markets?

DAVID BAHNSEN: Well, when you have a beta that is about 0.6 to the market, you naturally have less sensitivity, by definition, to the market itself. The only two stocks in the Dow that were up in 2008 were Walmart and McDonald’s, which were two of the great dividend growers of the last 50 years. They tend to be much more defensive. However, I will also point out that in terms of the offense against inflation, there is no inflation if oil prices aren’t going higher, if cheeseburgers don’t cost more, if soap and towels and Pepsi soda pop don’t cost more. So there’s an inherent inflationary benefit in the fact that the dividend growth has always, in every calendar year, been higher than whatever the growth of prices is — the inflation rate. If you’re getting a portfolio that’s growing dividends from six to 9% and inflation is somewhere between two and 5%, then you are by definition beating inflation in that cash flow. That is, to me, a very important element of the portfolio itself. Whether or not we go into recession, I think that this speaks to the sort of all-weather nature. There’s offense and defense involved in dividend growth.

The last time we had a bad market that was long term — not just the 30 days of COVID or the five days of Liberation Day, but you recall very well both — dot-com lasted two and a half years, from 2000 to 2002; the financial crisis, the market drop was 18 months. And in that period, the S&P was up, from 2000 to 2009, 0%. Most dividend growth portfolios would’ve been up somewhere in the range of seven, 8% per year. So I think that it is a very good time to be looking at it.

Now, what’s a fair question is: hey, but how much did I lose in opportunity cost? The 2009 to 2026 bull market, the S&P’s compounded 15% a year. It doesn’t do me any good to make three or 4% in your stupid dividends while I’m missing that. The fact of the matter is, about half of those years dividend growth has done better than the market. Half of them, not as much. But it’s right there in the same range in a screaming bull market for the index, a screaming low-volatility period where the yield of the S&P is at the lowest it’s ever been.

BARRY RITHOLTZ: Really, really interesting. One of the criticisms I’ve heard made about dividend growth investing is sometimes investors confuse receiving cash with creating wealth. The classic example is buying a stock right before the dividend issuance, and when it goes ex-dividend, the price falls by the amount of the dividend that gets paid. Tell us what this criticism misses. What’s the mistake there?

DAVID BAHNSEN: Yeah, but when people do that, they fail to understand how markets work. It’s almost like a Treasury Secretary thinking he can buy 30-year bonds and the bond market won’t figure out how these things work.

BARRY RITHOLTZ: I just had that conversation earlier today. I’m like, aren’t you the world’s biggest issuer of debt? How is a tiny announced buyback going to do anything to the long end of that? But go on.

DAVID BAHNSEN: But of course, our Treasury Secretary was himself a global macro trader, and the mentality you bring up about trying to arbitrage dividend payments is something that short-term traders would do as well. So it’s a fine mentality for traders, but it’s a silly mentality in terms of the long-term impact in macroeconomic reality. It doesn’t arbitrage anything to go buy a dividend when markets are pricing in those realities and the algorithmic nature of things can pick up on it ahead of time, et cetera. You are not buying the timing of the receipt of a dividend. You’re buying the company’s underlying growth. You can’t fool the fundamentals.

So I would argue, Barry, that non-dividend investors are doing this far more than dividend investors. Fundamentally, most people that right now believe, “I want to buy the market because there’s someone else who thinks the market’s going to do well. I want to buy Nvidia because there’s someone else who thinks Nvidia’s going to do well” — even if it’s not fully self-conscious, the portfolio strategy of many investors today is dependent on what they think other people will do. Dividend growth investing says I’m isolated to it. I don’t even really need to look at the prices on my screen that much. I believe in the companies executing, growing profits, and growing what they return of that to me over time. And all these other arbitrage things — day by day, week by week, or in some cases nanosecond by nanosecond — are irrelevant to the long-term value creation.

3566f644ebabc6e6: Lifting has been around long before Gen Z. Frances Benjamin Johnston/ Library of Congress/ public domainMore than one quarter of young adults in Britain now say their gym memberships matter more to them than holidays or eating out. Sport England data shows that Gen Z has begun to turn away from running, swimming and fitness classes towards gym and strength training. For them, weight training is seen as the best form of exercise because it can help build strength, improve appearance and boost overall health. People have argued about the best forms of exercise for over two centuries. While today’s fitness trends tend to be more about improving the body and overall fitness, health has rarely been the sole reason why certain exercise trends gained popularity through the eras. Napoleon and gymnastics In 1806, Napoleon Bonaparte invaded Prussia and, inadvertently, created the modern fitness industry. As Napoleon’s troops stormed their way eastward, one Prussian man, Friedrich Ludwig Jahn, began to seethe with anger. For Jahn, Prussian men had lost because they were physically weaker than the French. The nation’s solution, according to Jahn, lay not in muskets – but muscles. So in 1811 Jahn opened a Turnplatz – an open-air gymnasium. Young men ran, jumped, climbed ropes, wrestled and vaulted. They also swung on two pieces of equipment that Jahn is believed to have invented: the parallel bars and the horizontal bar. Soon the trend spread to other nations, with England’s first outdoor gymnastics school opening in 1825. The underlying logic behind Jahn’s Turnplatz system – that strong nations demanded physically strong troops – became a rallying cry for a wave of gymnastic and calisthenic systems for men and women across the century. The birth of bodybuilding A popular form of entertainment in the Victorian era were strongmen shows, where muscular men would perform theatrical acts of strength. One of the most popular performers of the time was Charles “Samson” Sampson, whose act involved snapping chains with his chest. Eugen Sandow became synonymous with the ideal body. The Strobridge Lith. Co., Cin'ti & New York/ Wikimedia Commons But in 1889, a new kind of strongman arrived on the scene. During one of Sampson’s performances, a moustachioed strongman named Eugen Sandow stripped down to his pants in a London theatre, responding to a challenge from Sampson. But what made Sandow different from Sampson and other strongmen of the era was his physique. He was lean and sculpted. From 1889 until his death in 1925, Sandow became synonymous with the ideal body. He was deemed the “best specimen of manhood” by Harvard University physical educationalist Dudley Sargent. Sandow hosted the first major bodybuilding contest in London in 1901 and ran a health enterprise which spread across the British Empire, the Americas and Australasia. Thousands followed his mail-order courses, read his magazine and drank his cocoa. Those lifting dumbbells and barbells to build their bodies like Sandow classed themselves as “physical culturists” in the same way that modern trainees may define themselves by Pilates, Hyrox or weight training. Following Sandow and others, people trained for health but they also trained to become better workers, better spouses, to be more attractive or dynamic. Read more: Fitness gurus and ‘muscular Christianity’: how Victorian Britain anticipated today’s keep fit craze Although the state still mattered – Sandow even trained British troops for the second South African war – the emphasis slowly shifted to building the body for its own sake. The post-war aerobics boom The approach to exercise in the post-war era shifted due to an emerging new health concern: people were sitting down too much. This fear was fuelled by a 1953 work published by epidemiologist Jerry Morris which found that London bus drivers experienced higher instances of heart disease than conductors, who spent their day climbing stairs. The cause? Inactivity. In the US, physicians began rallying against rising heart disease. Their radical solution was to advise people to run slowly for set periods of time – an activity we today call jogging. Pioneered in New Zealand and brought to the US in the 1960s, jogging soon kickstarted an “aerobics” boom. New gym chains filled up with previously untrained enthusiasts running and doing aerobics classes. Aerobics classes were particularly popular with women. And in 1969, fitness instructor Jacki Sorenson originated the aerobics dance movement after she began setting routines to pop music, stitching together steps from jazz, folk, cha-cha and square dancing. Jacki Sorensen pioneered the aerobic dance movement. Employee of Aerobic Dancing, Inc./ Wikimedia Commons The popularity of aerobics only continued to grow throughout the 80s, thanks to actor Jane Fonda’s best-selling 1982 workout video which brought aerobics into the living room. The muscle builders In 1977 the world was introduced to Austrian bodybuilder Arnold Schwarzenegger in the hit documentary Pumping Iron. Brash but charming, muscular but beautiful, Schwarzenegger and the entrepreneur pushing him, Joe Weider, popularised bodybuilding as we now understand it. Pumping Iron hit cinemas at a time when aerobics had driven more people into gyms and new gym equipment made lifting weights far more accessible. Schwarzenegger’s physique soon became a template for heroic figures in pop culture. Action stars, children’s toys and athletes all succumbed to the bodybuilding effect. Leading 80s megastar Sylvester Stallone even transformed his body with Schwarzenegger’s training partner Franco Columbu in preparation for Rambo and the Rocky movies. Women were lifting, too. Lisa Lyon won the first women’s world bodybuilding championship in 1979. Two decades later women’s weightlifting reached the Olympics. By the 2000s, lifting weights was no longer a fringe activity. Budget and 24-hour gyms were commonplace while sports such as CrossFit and powerlifting swelled with men and women. In recent years the hashtag #strongnotskinny has spread across Instagram and TikTok. Exercise scientist Andrew Scott says that influencers have been a big part of this shift. None of this is new. Sandow sold his body on postcards and cocoa tins, Fonda sold hers on VHS and Schwarzenegger sold his at the cinema. Once again, the world around us is changing how people move their bodies. Two hundred years ago, fitness served the country. Now it serves the algorithm. DC Studio / ShutterstockRussian hostile activity costs the UK at least £2 billion annually, according to a recent report by Scottish MP Graeme Downie, who has called on the government to measure what these actions cost Britain. But this figure is just the baseline. In reality, a profound shift in Moscow’s approach to sabotage means the true cost is set to climb higher. While Russia still draws on its cold war target lists, ranging from critical transit nodes and military sites; to energy and communication infrastructure; it has traded highly trained operatives for cheap technology and expendable recruits. The switch to a quantity-over-quality model presents a much more volatile threat. This model borrows from the logic of distributed computing. It uses networks of cheap, unreliable parts where individual breakdowns are expected yet the overall system still gets the job done. By generating a high volume of low-cost operations that often fail at the individual level, Moscow still achieves its objectives of causing outsized psychological disruption and steadily exhausting western security services. A 2024 arson attack on a London warehouse is one of a number of sabotage attempts European authorities believe Russia has ordered in recent years. This operational transformation surged after Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. Within months, over 400 Russian intelligence officers operating under diplomatic cover were expelled across Europe. This number has since climbed to more than 700. The mass purge was expected to cripple Russia’s spy networks. But it instead accelerated Moscow’s pivot towards what research I carried out with colleagues in 2024 defined as “gig-economy” operatives. In place of declared “diplomats” well known to local counterintelligence officers, operations have been outsourced to disposable proxies recruited for a pittance. These people are often unaware of who their handlers are or their mission’s real goals. This new campaign brings to life former CIA chief James Woolsey’s 1993 description of the post-cold war security landscape as a “jungle of venomous snakes”. Gig-economy operatives Recruited on messaging apps and paid in cryptocurrency, gig-economy operatives have been tasked with arson and other property damage, beatings, kidnappings and assassinations. This includes assassination plots on US soil in a stark breach of cold war conventions. While many of these plots have been amateurish, the intent behind them and their potential damage is real. Blurring the lines between theatrics and physical damage, the campaigns have included mock coffins placed beneath the Eiffel Tower and graffiti designed to stoke antisemitic tensions across Paris. Arson targets have ranged from a warehouse in London storing aid for Ukraine to an Ikea store in Lithuania and a paint factory in Poland. Western intelligence also narrowly averted catastrophe in 2025 when incendiary devices planted on DHL cargo planes caught fire in freight depots on the ground rather than mid-flight. Beyond commercial property, Moscow’s campaign has targeted critical infrastructure. At sea, the playbook has escalated from plausible deniability to overt military posturing. Since 2023, Russian-linked commercial vessels flagged from China to the Cook Islands have repeatedly severed power and data cables by dragging their anchors across the seabed. The Russian authorities have backed this with hard power. This has ranged from scrambling fighter jets to deter Estonian authorities from approaching a suspected vessel in 2025, to deploying intelligence ships and submarines close to western lines. A parallel escalation has unfolded in the air. Operations began with electronic interference and drone surveillance disrupting commercial aviation, as well as probing European military bases and transport hubs to test air defences and map blind spots and vulnerabilities. They have since graduated to overt airspace violations by Russian military aircraft and missiles, while armed drones have repeatedly crashed or detonated in Polish, Latvian and Moldovan territory. This pattern crossed from deniable sabotage into a direct physical attack in August 2026 when an explosives-laden drone crashed into the wing of a parked Ukrainian cargo plane at Leipzig/Halle Airport in Germany. The device failed to detonate, averting a major explosion on an aircraft that had previously transported military ammunition. The incident exposed not only Moscow’s escalatory ambitions, but also the sharp decline in professionalism within Russian intelligence. Rather than the elite officers cold war doctrine called for, the Russian intelligence handler relied on amateur recruits, who botched the job. Yet for Moscow, operational failures are almost as useful as successes. A botched strike still generates media panic, exhausts European security services and projects a menacing shadow far beyond Russia’s real capabilities. Moscow’s cyber campaigns The same logic underpins the Kremlin’s cyber campaigns, where merely threatening critical infrastructure is often enough to achieve intimidation. Cyberattacks on a Norwegian dam and a Swedish heating plant, both in 2025, caused negligible physical damage. But they generated alarming headlines and have had psychological effects. Also in 2025, a cyberattack on a major Polish power and heating plant threatened to cut heat to half a million people during winter. Even though blackouts were avoided, the destructive potential was impossible to ignore. In cyber operations, as in physical sabotage, the perpetrators range from opportunistic proxies like the pro-Russian hackers in Sweden to elite hacking units directed by Russian intelligence in Poland. Across domains, Russia has turned unpredictability and disruption into its strategic weapon of choice. Using expendable, poorly trained proxies directed remotely by state handlers consistently achieves psychological disruption while narrowly averting casualties through operational failure. However, relying on Russian incompetence to protect European lives cannot hold. As the old maxim goes: hope is not a strategy. 3b1852bb0011105e: Enterprise AI can generate recommendations, automate tasks, and help organizations make decisions faster. But without an understanding of how a business actually operates, even powerful models can miss the constraints and relationships that determine whether a decision is the right one. As companies look to move AI from experimentation into everyday operations, the challenge ahead is giving technology the context to act usefully within complex business processes.

For Devavrat Shah, chief scientist of enterprise AI at Celonis, that context is central to what he calls “decision intelligence.” AI agents can support individual tasks within larger decision-making processes, he argues, but they need to understand the role each task plays and the business conditions surrounding it. “You can’t just do that in a vacuum,” he says. Without the right operational context, agents risk overlooking important constraints, making costly mistakes, or consuming excessive computing resources as they try to work out what they need to know.

The solution begins with connecting AI to the processes and data enterprises already use. A contextual layer can help agents understand workflows, operate within defined guardrails, and produce recommendations that people can review and approve. Shah advises organizations to start with a specific business decision, identify its most difficult steps, and test whether AI can improve them. Measuring gains in speed and value can then help determine whether an application is worth scaling.

This approach could also change how employees spend their time. Automating repetitive, manual work and coordinating tasks across teams could free people to focus on more complex strategic decisions. Realizing that benefit, however, will require investment in workforce education, so employees can understand AI outputs and their implications instead of just handing decisions over to agents.

Looking to the future, Shah sees opportunities extending from routine operational tasks to enterprise-wide planning in areas such as finance, workforce management, marketing, and sales. With the right context, AI could help organizations evaluate options and make consequential decisions more quickly. As Shah puts it, “Now, maybe [resource planning] should not take that much time, and people are actually making the right choices quickly.”

Megan Tatum: From MIT Technology Review, I’m Megan Tatum, and this is Business Lab, the show that helps business leaders make sense of new technologies coming out of the lab and into the marketplace.

Now, enterprise AI is at something of a crossroads. By acting without operational context, enterprise AI and AI agents are performing at a significant deficit. They’re applying generalized principles to specialized scenarios and coming up short, leaving business leaders understandably unconvinced and AI’s potential unrealized.

My guest today is Devavrat Shah, chief scientist of enterprise AI at Celonis.
Welcome, Devavrat.

Now, it’s those tasks, or what I would call roles, that’s where AI can bring in an atomic manner agentic power so that we can at least parts of decisions, if not all of the decisions, we can augment support and maybe sometimes when it’s a painful automate. And to get to that, to know which role to do, which task to do, we really need to know the context. You can’t just do that in a vacuum. And that’s why context with AI put together in the right way would bring what I would call decision intelligence to enterprise. Megan: Right. To drill down into that into a bit more detail, we know many organizations are, as you say, embracing identic AI right now with this potential for increasingly autonomous decision making. If context isn’t introduced in parallel, what are the commercial risks at play?

The problem is to get to that, it will do so much compute at some level that to get simple tasks done, we are spending massive amount of compute. So that’s scenario one.

In reality, that’s not going to be the scenario, and we’ll miss some important context, important constraint, important guardrail, and then we’ll make a mistake. It’s like me giving you a recommendation saying, go restaurant A, and maybe you may not enjoy the dinner, versus sometimes mistakes will be very, very expensive. Megan: Right. So in an enterprise setting, these are really business critical decisions that are being made. So the impact is that much more if we get this wrong, isn’t it? Here are three things I took away.
Permafrost is a massive blind spot for climate change

Permafrost is the frozen layer of soil that’s under about 15% of land around the Northern Hemisphere. While technically material needs to be frozen for only two consecutive years to count as permafrost, most of our current permafrost formed during the last ice age.

That means there’s organic material that’s been frozen, and essentially locked away, for thousands of years. But as global temperatures tick up and this layer thaws, microbes are able to break down that organic matter, releasing carbon dioxide and methane—powerful greenhouse gases that drive climate change. Those emissions form a feedback loop, accelerating warming further.
The steady rise in global temperatures has already shrunk the footprint of the Arctic permafrost by about 12% since 1850, and the pace has been picking up in the last 50 years.

The wild thing is, only a minority of the models that have been used in UN climate reports actually take into account the gradual loss of permafrost. And none of them include the abrupt thaw and collapse that can happen after events like heat waves and fires (more on those fires in a moment). There are efforts to make sure future UN reports reflect the growing science, but for now, all this means that we’re probably underestimating how much and how fast the planet is going to warm.
Wildfires can speed up permafrost loss

Fire is a natural part of boreal forests’ life cycle, but they’re getting more intense because of climate change. And crucially, fires can accelerate the thawing of permafrost. By the end of the century, this effect could release the equivalent of 80 billion metric tons of carbon dioxide.

Today, the policy across remote parts of Canada and Alaska is generally to let wildfires burn as long as they’re not threatening human habitats. But some researchers say we should explore fighting these fires to save the carbon trapped in the forests and the permafrost beneath them.

Researchers at the Woodwell Climate Research Center are developing a map of burn risk and carbon vulnerability across Alaska, essentially highlighting areas where fires are most likely to spread and which areas are home to certain types of permafrost that would release the most emissions. (Yes, apparently there are different types of permafrost. Yedoma is a particularly deep, carbon-dense form from the late Pleistocene era.)

That’s all just the beginning—once we figure out potential targets, the question is what to do about it. Some suggest setting more prescribed fires, something Indigenous groups have done for thousands of years, partly to reduce the danger of massive blazes. Or resources could go to early detection and efforts to put out fires before they grow.
The carbon cycle of permafrost is incredibly complicated

There’s about 1.5 trillion tons of carbon locked away in permafrost, about twice the amount in the atmosphere. We know that permafrost thawing can release greenhouse-gas emissions and drive climate change. But there are complications.

One particularly big wrinkle: Other effects from permafrost thawing and fire recovery might counteract the carbon lost from those events. For example, as temperatures warm, plants can gradually move north and take hold where they couldn’t have before. Those plants soak up carbon from the atmosphere as they grow, at least partly locking away what was emitted.

Researchers are working to better understand this ecosystem. And the more we learn, the more complicated the picture looks. How much carbon is lost from permafrost, and how much a given area will recover its carbon, depend on a huge array of factors. How severe are the fires that have accelerated local thawing? What’s the local climate and environment? And what kind of permafrost is at stake?
The higher we push the planet’s temperature, the more we mess with complicated natural phenomena that we’re only beginning to understand.

8cacaf29b1375238: Ask most executives to picture the cost of AI and they’ll likely see GPUs—racks of accelerators with gigawatts of power—and a waitlist for silicon. But that picture leaves something out: Data storage costs.

What happens to data after a model responds? Much of the back-end data that’s generated—from billions of daily prompts, images, and videos—needs to be stored. But data storage is one of the harder infrastructure costs to plan for, and it’s often overlooked in initial AI infrastructure planning.
As inference scales, the data footprint grows with it

Traditionally, AI infrastructure conversations have centered on the compute-intensive process of training a model. Training is finite: a run starts, burns through compute, and ends. But inference runs continuously, every time a model answers a prompt. For infrastructure planning, that difference matters: A training run is a project you can budget for and retire. Inference doesn’t retire; every inference request leaves something behind.

Take AI-generated video. In this workload, the back-end spend can be significant. From internal measurements, WD found that an 8-second clip (returned to a user as a 3.97MB 720p file) left more than 500MB of associated data behind on the back end, including logs, cached context, immediate renders, backups, and safety records. That’s a 130x increase over the output file size the user saw. Scale this to an enterprise generating longer, higher resolution video and the back-end footprint grows into the hundreds of gigabytes per clip.

And that back-end footprint is growing fast. McKinsey projects AI inference demand will grow at a 35% CAGR through 2030, versus 22% for training, making up more than 40% of total data center demand by the end of the decade.

A recent WD-sponsored IDC global white paper that surveyed 763 IT and business decision makers found that nearly 95% of respondents reported an increase in data volume due to generative AI over the past 12 months, with roughly 61% reporting growth of 25% or more.

“You can think of having more storage as an optimization for keeping the GPUs busy,” said a senior product manager of a hyperscale cloud service provider quoted in report. “The biggest challenge is to ensure that the GPUs are not idle, waiting for data to show up—hours of GPU idle time becomes very expensive, very fast.” Put in dollar terms: if your storage spend is growing 25% year over year while your compute budget grows in the more predictable cyclical way, storage ends up outpacing the budget line that receives the most attention.
Matching storage to the AI data life cycle

Compute demand rises and falls with training cycles, product launches, and hardware refreshes. But the volume of retained data doesn’t fall back down with it when compute demand slows. Model logs, synthetic outputs, inference results, and more keep accumulating, and organizations are holding onto more of it for longer.

This changes the role of retained data. Information that once moved into an archive and rarely surfaced can now become an input to future AI workloads. As more data is retained, retrieved, and reused, storage must support not only growing capacity, but increasingly dynamic access to it. The same WD-IDC survey found 96% of respondents anticipate needing faster archive retrieval to support inference or retrieval-augmented generation (RAG).

AI workloads require both performance and capacity, with different technologies serving different needs across the data lifecycle. And for the vast volumes of data that must be retained and revisited, HDDs provide a cost-effective, high-capacity foundation, with a significant cost-per-terabyte advantage
What this means for how AI gets budgeted

For a CFO or CIO, this means “AI infrastructure spend” may be scoped too narrowly on compute. A model that idles while data loads costs about as much as one idling for lack of a GPU. But the storage bottleneck stays hidden until it’s already a problem, surfacing in operating costs and retrieval delays rather than a CapEx line next to the accelerators.

Consider a retailer generating AI product videos for its catalog, or an insurer running claims documents through a RAG pipeline for faster underwriting. In both cases, the compute cost is a known, budgeted quantity: a per-generation or per-query rate that finance can forecast. The storage cost is different: It compounds with every video generated and every claim processed, because none of that back-end data disappears once the task is finished.

A team that budgets AI as “compute plus a rounding error for storage” may find, in 12 to 18 months, that the rounding error has become a significant fraction of the program’s total cost—right around the time leadership is deciding whether to expand.
Building for economically scalable capacity

Addressing this challenge starts with architecture. Storage strategy tends to be designed for expensive, hot-tier performance (for data accessed instantly and constantly), while most AI data by volume accumulates in the warm, cool, and cold tiers behind it.

What enterprises need is economically scalable capacity: Infrastructure designed for the full AI data life cycle, balancing performance with capacity, power, reliability, and total cost of ownership as data persists, compounds, and is increasingly reused. That means treating archives that once sat untouched as active assets for RAG and inference, and setting retention policies for data’s growing strategic value rather than its original storage cost. It also means recognizing that decisions about storage play out across fleets, not individual drives.

Such infrastructure requires storage tiers, where individualized power consumption, reliability, density, and operational efficiency all determine whether the system remains economically sustainable as capacity scales.
There are three questions to ask about your organization’s AI infrastructure budget:
What’s our data retention policy for AI-generated content, and who set(s) it?
Is our storage procurement tied to training-time performance needs, or to the actual life cycle of the data we’re producing?
If our AI usage doubled next year, would our storage cost double with it, or worse?
Most organizations cannot answer all three with confidence. That’s the gap worth closing before the next budget cycle, not after.

dc2ecfeed8750825: From Moaz Nair

The persistent, fractured politicking among Indian political leaders has devolved into a tragic spectacle of self-preservation, birthing a swarm of toothless, ego-driven factions that have completely abandoned the community’s most vulnerable.
For decades, these leaders have traded genuine community advancement for personal clout and minor cabinet crumbs, leaving working-class Indians politically homeless.

Ironically, as the Indian demographic footprint shrinks, the number of these redundant, self-serving political groups keeps multiplying — each shouting from its own small hill while achieving absolutely nothing of substance.

If these career politicians truly possess an ounce of genuine care for the marginalised, they must immediately halt their petty bickering, dismantle their hollow factions, and focus on delivering institutional, non-negotiable economic welfare.

Recent demographic data from the statistics department covering 2016 to 2026 lays bare a damning reality. In just one decade, the Indian component of the citizen population shrivelled from 7% to 6.5%. Representing roughly 5.8% of the total national population, ethnic Indians total about 2.1 million citizens.
Behind these dwindling percentages lies an unsettling truth: a minority community is fast becoming adrift from the mainstream of national development.

Approximately 38.7% of the community falls into the Bottom 40% (B40) income bracket, translating to 227,000 households. More alarming still, the data indicates that 10% of these B40 families — around 22,000 households — survive on less than RM2,000 a month in extreme precarity.
However, a shrinking population footprint must never be used as a political excuse for a diminished national commitment.

Instead, this demographic decline demands an immediate paradigm shift — shattering the status quo of lazy, generic handouts and replacing them with high-impact policy interventions built upon three non-negotiable pillars.
The 2027 budget attempts to tackle these imbalances, but its success will hinge on execution.
Equity, asset ownership, and economic empowerment

A shrinking population share inherently dilutes purchasing power and locks minority communities out of wealth accumulation. To bridge this widening wealth chasm, outdated asset ownership policies must be aggressively dismantled.
This means enforcing strict, mandatory quotas and dedicated housing funds to guarantee B40 Indian households affordable housing.
The 2027 budget confronts these capital deficits by channelling a combined RM150 million through Tekun Nasional and Amanah Ikhtiar Malaysia.

This includes a dedicated RM100 million Indian Community Entrepreneur Development Scheme to provide critical capital to small business owners, and RM50 million in microcredit loans customised to uplift Indian women entrepreneurs.
Ensuring families own homes and hold financial assets is vital to systematically engineering sustainable, multi-generational social mobility.
TVET overhaul and educational infrastructure

A radical technical and vocational education and training (TVET) overhaul and digital empowerment must disrupt a stagnant workforce. The brutal job market of tomorrow will show no mercy to obsolete skillsets.
Indian youth — particularly those trapped in forgotten suburban fringes and estates — must be aggressively channelled into high-tier TVET ecosystems.

The 2027 budget offers a vital fiscal upgrade here. The allocation for the Malaysian Indian Transformation Unit (Mitra) has been boosted to RM150 million, specifically earmarked to help youths make the transition into high-skilled industrial pipelines. Furthermore, Indian youth must tap into the wider national RM8 billion TVET budget.

Equally foundational is confronting the historical deficits in education infrastructure. Malaysia’s 528 Tamil national-type primary schools (SJKT) carry a complex legacy, with 324 operating as government-assisted institutions sitting on private estate or community trust lands.

This has historically locked many schools out of direct development funding, leaving 68% of them without basic ICT laboratories. The 2027 budget addresses this digital divide with a RM50 million allocation for essential repairs, rewiring, and basic amenities, alongside full reconstruction priorities for severe emergencies like at SJKT Dengkil in Selangor and SJKT Gopeng in Perak.
Ruthless structural reform for targeted poverty alleviation
The survival of these policies hinges entirely on a ruthless structural reform of Mitra. For decades, fragmented agendas and redundant aid distribution have sabotaged state interventions.

Mitra must be stripped of bureaucracy and given absolute, transparent, and centralised power over data, funding, and execution. Armed with a unified database, cost-of-living aid, scholarships, and micro-business grants can finally bypass bureaucratic gridlock.

Crucially, the ultimate success of the budget for working-class Indians relies on broader macroeconomic shifts. The mandated minimum wage hike to RM2,000 per month starting June 2027 will immediately lift the community’s most vulnerable 22,000 households out of deep financial distress, especially when combined with the RM16 billion Sumbangan Tunai Rahmah cash aid pool.
Moving beyond salvation

Ultimately, the integrity of Malaysia’s future will be judged by how it treats its most vulnerable. Addressing this demographic collapse is not a bloodless numbers game on a spreadsheet; it is an urgent battle for socioeconomic justice.
By executing these progressive policy pillars, the country can transform a demographic challenge into a powerful reservoir of human capital.

However, relying solely on external political salvation is a failing strategy. If the Indian community is to survive as a relevant economic force in Malaysia’s shifting landscape, it must aggressively dismantle internal fatalism.

Upward mobility cannot be granted by policy alone. Real transformation demands that the community fiercely engineer its own self-upliftment — taking absolute ownership of its wealth, its trajectory, and its future generations.
Moaz Nair is an FMT reader.

002e5577aa298cd4: Untuk seketika, perkataan ‘paling bodoh’ menjadi kata kunci yang masyhur. Ini ekoran seorang siswi Fakulti Ekonomi daripada Universiti Malaya (UM) bernama Ummi Umairah Bakhit menyelar tindakan segelintir Melayu yang menderma wang hasil titik peluh untuk membantu golongan elit disabitkan kes rasuah. Ummi menyatakan perbuatan tersebut adalah sesuatu yang paling bodoh selain tidak bermoral. Kenyataan, atau lebih tepat soalan Ummi tersebut dilontarkan ketika acara dalam sebuah forum terbuka yang menampilkan panel antara lain seorang DJ terkenal, Menteri Besar Johor Onn Hafiz Ghazi dan Menteri Besar Selangor Amirudin Shari. Forum itu adalah sebahagian daripada acara Sidang Kemuncak Pemimpin Muda Masa Depan Antarabangsa di Kuala Lumpur.

Dalam pertanyaan Ummi itu, beliau mempersoalkan tindakan sesetengah orang yang memilih menderma bagi membantu pesalah rasuah, Najib Razak, untuk membayar denda mahkamah berjumlah RM50 juta bagi membolehkan dirinya layak menjadi tahanan di rumah. Suis ketokohan Onn Hafiz nampak off atau terpadam seketika manakala DJ terkenal dalam forum tersebut nampaknya tersangkak, gugup lagi gagap untuk menjawab soalan yang tidak dijangka itu.

Bukan sahaja kata bodoh, sebetulnya Ummi mempertikaikan tindakan mempertahankan rasuah dan korupsi dengan menyebut-nyebut perihal skandal Tabung Haji dan lain-lain. Ini adalah intipati yang sepatutnya menjadi sorotan.

Meskipun berbahasa Inggeris, kata bodoh yang digunakan memang menular menjadi racun dalam pembuluh darah ramai penyokong Najib. Selepas keratan video itu menjadi tular, ramai dalam kalangan ahli Umno di media sosial ‘menghunus keris’ kepada siswi ini. Ada yang malah meminta Universiti Malaya mengambil tindakan terhadap beliau. Ummi malah diugut, diancam dan dinista. Padahal kata-kata Ummi menistai perbuatan rasuah itu adalah sesuatu yang terpuji.

Setelah ancaman terhadap Ummi menjadi-jadi, Menteri Pendidikan Tinggi Zambry Abdul Kadir akhirnya menegaskan mahasiswa mempunyai hak untuk bersuara dan tiada sebarang tindakan tatatertib akan dikenakan terhadapnya susulan pertanyaan kritis mengenai dana sumbangan Najib itu. Noor Azuan Abu Osman, naib canselor Universiti Malaya turut terpaksa tampil memberikan kenyataan rasmi yang senada.

Kenyataan kedua-dua tokoh besar dalam pengajian tinggi ini amat penting. Ini kerana bekas naib canselor Universiti Malaya antara tahun 1988 sehingga 1991, Syed Hussein Alatas iaitu seorang pemikir, yang karya masyhurnya bertajuk ‘Rasuah: Sifat, Sebab dan Fungsi’ pernah mempopularkan satu terma berkesan. Terma tersebut ialah gejala bebalisme. Ia datang daripada kata bebal, yang secara mudahnya bermaksud bodoh. Malah bebal adalah lebih dahsyat daripada bodoh. Ia adalah satu kalimat yang menunjukkan tumpul otak, sukar mengerti, lambat menanggapi atau memahami sesuatu perkara, dan menurut Dewan Bahasa dan Pustaka membawa juga pengertian melakukan aneka kesalahan berulang.

Akan tetapi apakah yang dimaksudkan oleh Syed Hussein yang terkenal benci rasuah dan perasuah itu dengan kata ‘bebal’. Beliau mula memperkenalkan istilah bebalisme dalam Dewan Masyarakat edisi Mac 1988.

Menurut Syed Hussein, bebalisme ini ‘bukan satu ideologi atau sistem kepercayaan atau kebudayaan atau falsafah’ tetapi ia adalah ‘orientasi pemikiran yang malas, tidak berfikir, tidak berlogik, kadang-kadang kasar, tidak ambil tahu, terlalu cepat percaya tanpa bukti, tidak saintifik, berhamburan, tiada haluan, pasif, tidak kreatif dan tiada tujuan yang terang.’

Semua anasir yang beliau sebutkan di atas akan kita jumpa di media sosial. Kita akan temukan di Facebook, X, Tiktok dan Threads. Apa sahaja yang disalurkan akan diulas sebagai satu komentar, atau ditelan bulat dan lonjong tanpa sebarang daya kritis. Tuduhan, fitnah, dakwaan palsu membiak dan beranak pinak dengan mudah di musim politik bergelora. Gejala bebalisme ini akan mudah dieksploitasi oleh pihak bertentangan dalam politik. Masing-masing akan menyebar informasi yang entah ya entah tidak.

Syed Hussein seterusnya mengatakan ‘bebalisme adalah lintah bagi pemikiran’. Ia tidak perlu diajarkan, atau dikemukakan secara teratur. Ia terjadi dengan sendiri dan ‘disebarkan sebagai satu trend’ dan ia dirujuk sebagai lintah oleh beliau lantaran pelaku atau si bebalis itu ‘bertindak melalui mental tanpa kesedaran’.

Oleh sebab ia adalah lintah bagi pemikiran, ia boleh melekap pada siapa pun. Kata Syed Hussein, ia ‘berada dalam berbagai-bagai golongan masyarakat; tidak kira umur, jantina, kebudayaan, bangsa, agama, falsafah, keadaan, waktu dan tempat’.

Apa yang menggerunkan ia adalah unsur utama yang menghalang pertumbuhan intelektual. Makanya, apabila penyokong Umno ramai-ramai ingin membantai Ummi, kita segera tahu dan mengesani bahawa rata-rata orang Umno ini terkait dengan fenomena bebalisme yang membimbangkan ini. Mungkin tidak semua, misalnya Zambry yang juga ahli Umno.
Syed Hussein juga mengaitkan bebalisme dengan ‘aliran fanatik’ iaitu mereka yang enggan menerima kebenaran dan fakta, dan terus-terusan memilih untuk percaya hal-hal bodoh dan tanpa dasar.
Apakah ciri-ciri bebalisme dan mereka yang menghidapinya, iaitu bebalis?

Menurut Syed Hussein, sang bebalis itu adalah; pertamanya mempertahankan kejahilan dan kedegilan. Keduanya mereka itu pemalas, enggan mengikuti hujah dan menganalisanya. Ketiganya, mereka selalunya bersikap acuh tak acuh, berbanding dengan daya usaha yang gigih dalam berfikir. Yang mana apa sahaja lambakan penipuan dan perdaya akan ‘diterima, berbagai-bagai pendapat, berbagai-bagai khurafat, berbagai- bagai keanehan dan keganjilan’.

Keempat, bebalisme ini menjelma kerana ada rasa diri itu ‘bersifat berkuasa benar (authoritarian) yang mana ini benar pada sesetengah ahli politik yang berasa mereka masih berkuasa atau lebih berkuasa dari rakyat. Itulah sebabnya dalam hal Ummi kita melihat beliau dibuli di dalam talian.
Kelima, mereka yang bebal itu ‘tidak suka merenung dan berfikir dan tidak suka menguji (non-experimental)’.

Keenamnya, tambah Syed Hussein, ‘satu ciri bebalisme adalah menghendaki orang lain mempercayai apa yang disarankan atau diperkatakan tanpa memberi sebab-sebab atau penjelasan yang cukup mengenai sesuatu yang luar daripada kebiasaan’.

Ketujuh, Syed Hussein sosiologis terkemuka negara pernah menulis, ‘bebalisme tidak suka kepada sifat teratur dan perbahasan secara rasional dan tidak menghargai kedua-duanya sama sekali. Apabila seorang bebalis bertindak secara rasional, ini adalah kerana pengaruh daripada kebiasaan dan bukan pemikiran mendalam secara rasional dan kerana terapan agama atau kuasa luar.’ Jika kita merenung ciri ini, kita akan mendapati terdapat sesetengah penyokong agamawan atau tokoh kanan tertentu gagal berfikir waras kerana hati serta penglihatan mereka telah dibutakan oleh ketaasuban.

Kelapan, golongan bebal ini akan cepat kita kesani iaitu ’apabila mereka bertanya, ia menampakkan kurangnya kefahaman mereka tentang prinsip-prinsip dan dengan itu soalan mereka menjadi sia-sia.’ Sebagai contoh dalam hal isu kepimpinan adat dan pertikaian kedudukan Yamtuan Besar Negeri Sembilan Tuanku Muhriz Tuanku Munawir, apa sahaja fakta yang dibawa bahawa Undang yang lama telah digantikan di Luak dan disahkan di Dewan Keadilan akan kekal dinafikan, dipermainkan dan ditolak. Mereka enggan berusaha mempelajari prinsip adat sedia ada, dan terus-terusan menghasut, memprovokasi dan mencabar institusi adat dan diraja di negeri itu.

Dan kesembilan, Syed Hussein mengatakan sang bebalis itu biasanya ‘antilogik, kusut pemikiran, subur dengan kurafat, tidak mengandungi rasa seni (unaesthetic), tidak mempunyai sikap memelihara, menerima segala sesuatu tanpa menimbang dengan akal, tidak mempedulikan hukum sebab (causation) dan hukum pertentangan (contradiction), bersikap kuasa-benar (authoritative), dan pemikiran malas, degil, serta buntu.’

Jika kita khuatir gejala bebalisme ini mewabak di Malaysia, kita perlu mengetahui mana asal puncanya. Apakah yang menyebabkan bebalisme ini? Menurut Syed Hussein ia bermula di rumah. Tulis beliau dalam rencana itu, ‘penghalang yang pertama ialah suasana di rumah'. Dalam erti kata lain, jika ibu bapa bodoh dan bengap, biasanya mereka gagal menumbuhkan suasana tidak bebal dalam rumah tangga. Alatas malahan mengatakan untuk mengetahui rumah itu penuh kebebalan atau tidak, memadai dinilai jika ‘keluarga terlalu menggalakkan sukan dan muzik’ dan ‘tidak membaca buku’. Ini kerana ‘pengetahuan intelektual tidak disanjung tinggi sebagaimana pengetahuan tentang agama dan adat’. Syed Hussein seterusnya menyatakan bukanlah setiap rumah perlu melahirkan intelektual; ‘walaupun kita tidak mengharap tiap-tiap orang atau tiap-tiap keluarga melahirkan watak intelektual, tetapi kita perlu berharap sebahagian keluarga dan anggota masyarakat dapat menghasilkan semangat intelektual tadi’.
Apa yang lebih menakutkan dalam masyarakat adalah bebalisme ini turut dibiakkan oleh ahli akademik yang mana itu perlu dibincangkan dalam tulisan lain.

Misalnya, Ketua Menteri Melaka, Ab Rauf Yusoh bakal menerima ijazah kedoktoran daripada Universiti Kebangsaan Malaysia (UKM) pada 21 Nov ini. Ketua menteri Melaka yang bakal bergelar doktor itu pernah menyeru penyokong dan rakyat yang menyayangi Najib supaya mengumpulkan dana bagi membantu melengkapkan RM 50 juta agar beliau dapat ditahan di rumah.

Mujur sangat-sangat bekas ketua hakim negara, Tengku Maimun Tuan Mat dilantik sebagai penyandang pertama Kursi Diraja Integriti dan Tadbir Urus Baik, UKM. Pelantikan beliau itu diperkenan dan dititahkan oleh Yang Dipertuan Besar Negeri Sembilan, Tuanku Muhriz yang juga tersohor antirasuah dan korupsi.

Apa pun syukur nikmat Allah, ada Ummi Umairah Bakhit yang telah dididik dan diasuh di rumah yang betul, di sekolah yang betul, di universiti yang betul; dan membaca bahan-bahan yang betul sehingga mampu berfikir kritis dan tidak bodoh. Sebagai alumni Universiti Malaya saya berbangga dengan Ummi. Tambahan pengungkap kata Syed Hussein adalah sarjana di Universiti Malaya dan pernah menjadi felo penyelidik kanan di Institut Alam dan Tamadun Melayu (Atma) di UKM suatu masa dahulu.
Pun berapa ramai generasi baharu seperti Ummi Umairah Bakhit? Berapa ramai yang mengenali Syed Hussein Alatas. Buka media sosial anda dan lihat berapa dan betapa ramai bebalis di luar sana.

042dfe8c62606c77: Ilya Pavlov / UnsplashDetails have been published of a critical flaw in the programming language PHP, which is the backbone of more than 70% of all websites. Left unfixed, the flaw would allow hackers to easily take over and compromise millions of websites and the information held on their servers. In response, multiple European governments and operators including the Port of Rotterdam have taken websites offline. The Australian Signals Directorate, America’s Cyber Defence Agency, and similar bodies from the United Kingdom, Europe and Japan have all warned web developers to apply urgent updates to their core systems, and to consider taking down websites until safety can be guaranteed. The organisation behind the free, open-source language has published updates that patch the flaw, but performing the updates on the millions of systems that use PHP will take time. What is PHP? PHP is often called “the backbone of the web”. It’s a programming language – a way to give instructions to computers – that has been around since 1997, and it allows websites to manage user inputs and process information behind the scenes. The power of PHP is its versatility. Websites use it for everything from logging users into accounts and running online stores, to requesting data from databases and powering millions of blog posts and news sites. PHP runs on the server rather than your personal computer. This means most of us interact with PHP every single day without ever seeing it. A timeline of concerns In August, a cybersecurity researchers from a company called Wiz used their own tools and the latest versions of Google’s Gemini and OpenAI’s ChatGPT AI models to trawl through PHP’s massive codebase. The Wiz team were searching for hidden programming weaknesses that an attacker could chain together to take over a system running PHP simply by sending a carefully crafted request over the internet. Within a few days, they found ways to break into PHP-powered systems from Drupal and WordPress which are used in huge swathes of the web. Wiz contacted the PHP security team to let them know about the flaws they had found. By late September, the PHP developers confirmed that the issue existed, and quietly began working on a fix. In cybersecurity, the responsible thing to do when you find a bug is to keep it private until a patch is ready. This is because public disclosure could provide a detailed map for hackers to exploit. This appears to be what the PHP developers were planning. However, yesterday a user on popular industry website Hacker News let news slip about the security flaws before any patches were ready. Following the leak, PHP’s developers rushed to publicly confirm the issue on October 21, releasing emergency patches ahead of schedule. Implementing the patches is far from simple. Because PHP sits underneath thousands of third-party plugins, frameworks and managed hosting services, websites are only secure once every individual layer of the supply chain integrates and deploys the PHP fix. Why does this keep happening? Much of the internet is built on foundational technologies that were developed and maintained by hobbyist developers. Many rely on goodwill and donations rather than robust corporate funding. Many of these tools were first developed decades ago. They were never designed to safely support a world where millions of websites and billions of devices use them to handle sensitive and private data. Compounding this issue is the fact that maintenance is rarely a priority for organisations. All too often, companies have only the most basic knowledge about all the pieces of their supply chains – either physical or digital. Even in high profile cases such as this one, many businesses don’t even realise what software they depend on, let alone have any idea of how secure it actually is. What should you do? This issue is mainly one for people who maintain websites or manage technical infrastructure. For those people, the priority is clear: patch systems immediately when updates are available, and consider taking down critical systems from the internet until you can be confident about their security. For everyday internet users, these vulnerabilities affect the servers hosting websites rather than your personal device. However, because some sites may be temporarily compromised before they can patch, it is wise to be cautious about entering sensitive personal data on unfamiliar websites over the next few days. Major cloud providers and security firms are rolling out emergency filters, but the global scramble to secure the web is just beginning. Cybersecurity teams around the world are rushing to contain the damage. But the scope of this issue should be a wake-up call. Governments and businesses cannot ignore the resilience of their digital supply chains. Just as manufacturers track the suppliers of the physical components they depend upon, we should expect that digital infrastructure also traces every system and framework it depends on. Gathering this information is the first step for businesses and governments to truly understand how heavily their digital viability relies on underfunded, volunteer-maintained code. Until businesses treat funding open-source foundational tools as a critical security investment rather than a charity, these vulnerabilities will keep happening. Andrew Cullen is a board member at Music Technology Australia, a member of the World Intellectual Property Organizations AI Technical Exchange Committee, and the managing consultant at EthiCan.
e3f519129b2e62b1: Whenever a minimum wage announcement falls short of public expectations, the political knee-jerk reaction is to aim all arrows at Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim.
Yet, directing the blame solely at him misses the real dynamics behind Malaysia’s wage policy formulation.

First, consider how policy recommendations are shaped. Talent Corp and the human resources ministry paid RM1 million to a consulting firm specifically to research and recommend an appropriate minimum wage rate.
When the government relies on external subject-matter experts, paid handsomely with public funds, it acts on structured economic assessments rather than arbitrary political whims.
If the resulting figure feels inadequate to the working public, we must scrutinise the methodology, data and assumptions used by these highly paid consultants first.
The research, findings, and identity of these consultants ought to be made public for full transparency and proper scrutiny before rushing to condemn the prime minister.

Second, the relentless pushback from employer groups continues to stall wage growth. Business associations and industry groups routinely lobby against wage increases, warning of economic ruin and mass layoffs.

Their aggressive pushback invariably leads to exemptions and now deferred compliance for micro, small, and medium enterprises (MSMEs), diluting the impact of wage reforms across major sectors of the economy.
Meanwhile, Anwar’s track record demonstrates a consistent commitment to raising worker compensation.
The minimum wage has risen 33% under the Madani government from RM1,500 in 2022 to RM2,000 in 2027. Graduates and semi-skilled workers will have a new minimum monthly salary of RM2,500.

Under Anwar’s administration, government-linked companies (GLCs) have actively led by example, setting a baseline living wage that was raised in Budget 2027 from RM3,100 to RM3,400. This upward revision reflects a genuine drive to ensure decent standards of living where the government holds direct leverage.

The true obstacles to a higher floor wage are not found in the prime minister’s office. The real villains in this story are the corporate lobbies constantly fighting wage increases and the consultants who produce conservative recommendations despite million-ringgit fees.

Rather than make Anwar the scapegoat, public discourse should demand accountability from the consultants who drafted the proposal and the employer groups who consistently undermine fair pay for Malaysian workers.

That said, according to research and analysis published in The Economist, governments should be cautious about aggressive minimum wage hikes due to mounting evidence of hidden economic distortions and better alternative policy tools.

Research from Nobel Prize winner David Card and others in the 1990s showed that the negative impact of minimum wages was overstated and job-losses were offset by higher spending and economic activity.

Recent studies, such as evaluations of sharp minimum wage increases in places like Seattle, show that high-wage floors can slow down the hiring of low-wage workers and reduce total work hours rather than cause immediate mass layoffs.
To offset higher baseline pay, employers often resort to unpredictable scheduling, fewer workplace perks, or higher output demands that can lead to increased workplace accidents.
High minimum wages are a blunt tool for fighting poverty because many minimum-wage earners live in households with high-earning family members.
Businesses, especially in labour-intensive or low-margin sectors, frequently pass higher wage costs onto consumers through rising prices, triggering affordability pressures.

The Economist highlights alternatives such as in-work tax credits, the progressive wage policy (PWP) in Malaysia or reverse income taxes, as superior approaches because they target low-income households directly without creating the same economic distortions or hidden costs.
Regular readers of this column will be familiar with these ideas because I have advocated them for many years and they have recently been adopted by Bersama.

The warning, obtained by 404 Media, was issued by the Orange County Intelligence Assessment Center (OCIAC)—a government fusion center—in July to police in California. 404 Media recently obtained the bulletin using a Freedom of Information Act request.

This surveillance bulletin to cops is the latest evidence that police around the country have been told to be on edge during public meetings where people are participating in democracy and utilizing their First Amendment rights about unpopular things the government is doing. We have reported on a spate of people being illegally arrested for extremely minor procedural violations or for cursing at city council meetings about Flock and data centers while participating in constitutionally protected activities.

The warning is similar to others obtained by 404 Media and other journalists about the broader DeFlock movement and vandalism of Flock surveillance cameras. But this warning specifically tells police that there have been “no specific and credible threats found” related to city council meetings about Flock, but warns they should be on the lookout anyway. “City-hosted events (i.e., city council meetings) may be viewed by extremists as a desirable target. Partners are encouraged to review for signs of suspicious activity,” the warning reads. Here is a full excerpt of the portion of the warning about protected activities that could apparently “present public safety risks:”

Large turnout exceeding room capacity: If organizers mobilize significantly more attendees than the council chambers can accommodate, this can lead to long lines, frustrated attendees, overflow areas, or delays in the meeting.

Emotional confrontations: Because the issue involves surveillance, privacy, immigration concerns, and public safety, speakers and attendees may have strong emotions. Verbal confrontations between supporters and opponents are more likely than at routine council meetings.

Experts say there are working exploits for the flaws, and that these critical bugs are already being exploited in the wild.

The flaws at issue are present in PHP, the programming language that powers sites running on a large number of web publishing systems, including Drupal, Magento, Joomla and WordPress. Earlier today, PHP released an emergency security update to fix two critical bugs that can allow an attacker to execute code of their choosing on a vulnerable server.

Cloudflare said it has already detected some exploitation of the flaw, and that at 3:02 am (UTC) it implemented web application firewall rules to protect websites from attack traffic seeking to exploit the bugs, which could cause a denial of service condition, remote code execution, and data exposure.

OpenAI, which was involved in the vulnerability research and outreach, said “given the severity of these flaws and PHP’s widespread use, we consider this one of the most impactful security issues in recent memory.”
Censys, a company that tracks the technology used by Internet hosts, said a recent scan identified approximately 2.58 million Internet facing hosts and 54.9 million web properties running PHP.
Security experts at Wiz said every PHP version released in the last decade is affected by at least one of these vulnerabilities [full disclosure: Wiz is an advertiser on this blog].

“These findings rank among the most severe vulnerabilities discovered in PHP, and arguably in software history,” reads a blog post published today by a team of researchers at Wiz, which was one of several organizations credited with discovering the vulnerabilities. “The underlying flaws had been present for decades, but demonstrating their exploitability required an exceptionally complex chain of steps, at the edge of what human researchers could practically achieve. Frontier AI models substantially reduced that barrier, turning a longstanding flaw into an exploit.”

The Wiz researchers say it is likely the PHP vulnerabilities will be mass-exploited to install web-based backdoors or “web shells,” which give attackers a web-based panel that allows them to remotely control infected sites. Wiz said that prior to the PHP bugs being publicly disclosed, the company worked with the PHP team, Calif and OpenAI to measure the size of the problem and coordinate patch verification and disclosure.

The PHP zero-day vulnerabilities are being tracked by their CVE numbers, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, and they affect all web servers running PHP 5.4 or later. The bugs are fixed in PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, and 8.2.35.

According to Wiz, PHP is so deeply embedded in many web applications that we are likely to see organizations struggling to patch these vulnerabilities for some time to come, comparing this PHP vulnerability pair with the Log4Shell weakness that emerged in 2021 — a widespread, severe-as-it-gets security flaw in Log4j, a popular Java logging framework.

“A vulnerability in core PHP reaches far beyond a single application,” the Wiz researchers wrote. “PHP runs across clouds, hosting providers, content-delivery networks and millions of independently managed servers. Reducing exposure before the technical details became public required coordinated work across that entire ecosystem.”

The SANS Internet Storm Center is keeping an eye on major software platforms that are shipping updates to deal with these PHP flaws. For example, Ubuntu just released updated PHP packages.
